name: Grade 3
theme: The Commandments and the Beatitudes: living as God’s children

units.title: God’s plan of love
units.eq: How does God show his love?

lessons.title: God speaks to us
lessons.idea: God wants us to know him, so he speaks to us: in the beauty of creation, through the prophets, and most fully in his Son, Jesus. The Bible is God’s word written down by people he inspired, and the Church helps us understand it.
lessons.question: How does God speak to us today?
lessons.activity: “Ways God speaks” stations (20 min). Station 1: look at a leaf, a shell or a photo of stars and write “God shows us…”. Station 2: read Psalm 19:1–4 aloud in pairs. Station 3: read John 1:14 and draw Jesus as God’s Word. Rotate every 5 minutes. End by sharing one thing each station taught.
teach: Revelation means God showing us who he is (CCC 50–53). He did it step by step: creation, Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses, the prophets, and finally Jesus, his Word made flesh (CCC 65).
Hebrews 1:1–2 gives the whole story in two verses: “In many and various ways God spoke… but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.” Read it slowly with the class.
God is the author of the Bible and the human writers were real authors too (CCC 105–106). Say “inspired” means God breathed his message through them without taking away their personality.
Watch for the idea that the Bible fell from the sky or that Catholics do not read it. The Church reads it at every Mass and invites everyone to read it daily.
talk: How do you get to know a friend?
Where do you see God’s work in creation?
Which part of the Bible have you heard?
quiz: God reveals himself most fully in…|A dream|His Son, Jesus|A rock|A book only|1|Hebrews 1:1-2.
The Bible is God’s word in…|Secret code|Human words|Songs only|Pictures|1|CCC 105-106.
Revelation means…|A mystery story|A test|God showing himself|A secret|2|CCC 50-53.
lessons.life: Read one Gospel story with a parent this week and ask: “What does this show me about God?”
lessons.saint: Jerome: he spent his life translating the Bible so people could know Christ.
misc: “God only spoke to people long ago.”
“The Bible is just an old storybook.”
lessons.mem: Hebrews 1:1–2 (first part): “In many and various ways God spoke… but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.”
lessons.hook: Hold up a letter with a stamp and a sunset photo. Ask: “How do you find out what someone is like?” Friends tell us, show us, and are with us. God does all three: he made a world full of signs, he spoke through prophets, and he sent Jesus.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name two ways God speaks to us and give one example of each.

script.open: Whisper a message to one child and have it passed around the circle, until the last child says it aloud. Notice how it changed. Then say, “It is hard to pass a message accurately. But when God wants to tell us something, he does it perfectly. Let’s see how.”
teach: Say: “God wants us to know him. A friend tells you about himself, and God does the same. We call this Revelation, which means ‘uncovering.’ How has God spoken to us? First, through creation: when we look at the stars, a mountain or a baby, we see that someone great made them. Psalm 19 says, ‘The heavens declare the glory of God.’”

Say: “Second, God spoke through the prophets, such as Moses, Isaiah and Jeremiah, who gave God’s messages to the people. And third, and most fully, he spoke through his Son. The letter to the Hebrews says: ‘In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.’ Jesus is God’s Word made flesh.”

Say: “The Bible is God’s word written down. God inspired real human authors to write what he wanted, so the Bible has both God and people as its author. The Bible is like the Holy Spirit’s book. And the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, helps us understand it correctly, which is why we read the Bible with the Church. When we hear Scripture at Mass, God is speaking to us.”
ask: Name three ways God speaks to us. (Creation, prophets, Jesus; also the Bible and Church.)
Why is Jesus called the Word of God? (He is God’s fullest message to us, God himself in person.)
Who helps us understand the Bible? (The Church, led by the Holy Spirit.)
practice: Set up four stations: Creation (a leaf, a shell or photos of stars), Prophets (a pictured scroll with a short quote from Isaiah 9:6), Jesus (a crucifix and a Gospel), and the Bible (a Bible open to Psalm 19).
Give each child a station sheet with four prompts: “God shows me…”, “God told his people…”, “God spoke to us in…”, “God speaks today by…”.
Rotate every five minutes; children write one sentence at each station.
Return to the circle, and share one thing each child discovered.
script.close: Read Psalm 19:1 aloud: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” Say: “Thank you, God, for speaking to us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read one Bible verse tonight with your family.”

tryit: Visit each station: creation, the prophets, Jesus, the Bible.
Write what God shows you at each.
Share one with the class.
lessons.saintStory:
Jerome was born around the year 347 in what is now Croatia. He studied in Rome and was a brilliant student, and he loved the great Latin writers. But a dream made him think about what he loved most, and he decided to give his life to God’s word.
He went to live as a hermit in the desert, learned Hebrew, and then settled in Bethlehem, near the cave where Jesus was born. There he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew and the New Testament from Greek into Latin, the common language of the people. This translation, the Vulgate, was used by the Church for over a thousand years. Jerome had a hot temper and liked to argue. But he worked hard on the Bible for thirty-four years.
He wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.” Jerome shows us that the Bible is how God speaks to us, and it is worth our care.

lessons.title: The Bible: our holy book
lessons.idea: The Bible is a library of 73 books, 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Old Testament tells how God prepared the world for Jesus, and the New Testament tells about Jesus and the first Church. The Gospels are the heart of the Bible.
lessons.question: How many books are in the Bible?
lessons.activity: “Bible treasure hunt” (25 min). Give pairs a Bible and a list of 8 references (Genesis 1:1, Psalm 23:1, Isaiah 9:6, Matthew 5:3, Luke 2:11, John 3:16, Acts 2:1, Revelation 21:4). They find each, identify the section (Law, History, Wisdom, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, Letters, Revelation) and copy one phrase. Review how to read a reference: book, chapter, verse.
teach: The Catholic Bible has 73 books: 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New (CCC 120). The books are grouped by kind: Law, history, wisdom and psalms, prophets, Gospels, Acts, letters, Revelation.
The Church decided which books belong in the Bible, called the canon, guided by the Holy Spirit and by what the apostles handed on (CCC 120). The Old and New Testaments belong together (CCC 128–130).
The Gospels have a special place because they tell us about Jesus’ life and words (CCC 125). We stand when the Gospel is read at Mass to honor Christ himself speaking.
Teach reference reading as a skill. Many children have never opened a Bible. Let them practice and celebrate small wins.
talk: Which Bible story do you like?
Why is the New Testament about Jesus?
quiz: The Bible has…|73 books|100 books|27 books|10 books|0|CCC 120.
The Gospels tell about…|David|Moses|Jesus|Noah|2|CCC 124.
The Old Testament came…|After Christ|At Pentecost|Before Christ|In the 1900s|2|CCC 121.
lessons.life: Find your favorite Bible verse and write it on a card.
lessons.saint: Anthony the Great: a young man who heard the Gospel at Mass and changed his life.
misc: “Catholic Bibles have the same number of books as all other Bibles.”
lessons.mem: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” (Psalm 119:105)
lessons.hook: Bring a Bible and a stack of 73 index cards, or a bookshelf. Ask: “Is this one book or many?” Explain that it is like a family library: history, songs, letters, stories, prophecies, all about God’s love.
lessons.assess: Give each child a Bible and a reference to find. Watch their fingers: can they find book, chapter and verse?

script.open: Hold up the Bible and a small library book. Ask, “What is the difference between this book and a regular book? Is it long or short? Who wrote it?” Take guesses. “The Bible is not one book, but a whole library of books.”
teach: Say: “The Bible has 73 books. There are 46 in the Old Testament, and 27 in the New Testament. Some are history, some are poetry and songs, like the Psalms, some are wise sayings, some are letters, some are the words of prophets. The Old Testament tells the story of God’s people before Jesus, and how God prepared the world for him. The New Testament tells about Jesus and the first Church.”

Say: “The heart of the Bible is the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. ‘Gospel’ means ‘good news.’ They tell the story of Jesus’ life, death and Resurrection. We stand when the Gospel is read at Mass, because it is Jesus’ own words.”

Read 2 Timothy 3:16: “All Scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching.” Say: “That means God is the author. We use a table of contents to find books, and chapters and verses to find passages. ‘John 3:16’ means the Gospel of John, chapter 3, verse 16.”
ask: How many books are in the Bible? (73.)
What are the two parts called? (Old Testament and New Testament.)
What does ‘Gospel’ mean? (Good news.)
practice: Give pairs a Bible and a list of eight references: Genesis 1:1, Psalm 23:1, Isaiah 9:6, Matthew 5:3, Luke 2:11, John 3:16, Acts 2:1, Romans 8:28.
Show how to use the table of contents, then say, “Go!”
Pairs write the book, the testament it is in, and what the verse says.
Gather and share. Which verse is your favorite? Why?
script.close: Read John 3:16 together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find a Bible at home and look for your favorite verse.”

tryit: Race to find the Bible verses.
Tell your partner what each says.
Choose your favorite.
lessons.saintStory:
Anthony was born in Egypt around the year 251. His parents were wealthy Christians, but they died when he was about twenty, and he was left to care for his younger sister and a large property.
One Sunday at Mass he heard the Gospel being read, where Jesus said to the rich young man, “Go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” Anthony felt as if these words were meant for him. He gave away his land, provided for his sister, and went out into the desert to pray.
Many people followed him to the desert to learn how to live for God. He is called the father of monks. Anthony shows what can happen when we really listen to the Bible: one verse can change a life.

lessons.title: Covenant: God’s promise
lessons.idea: A covenant is a sacred promise that makes people into a family. God made covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses and David, and Jesus makes the new and everlasting covenant by giving his body and blood.
lessons.question: Which covenant is your favorite?
lessons.activity: “Covenant timeline” (25 min). On a long paper strip draw five markers: rainbow (Noah), stars (Abraham), tablets (Moses), crown (David), chalice (Jesus). For each, write God’s promise and the sign. Read Genesis 9:8–17 aloud and trace the rainbow. Close by reading the words of the Eucharistic cup from Luke 22:20.
teach: A covenant is more than a contract: it makes people family (CCC 56–64). God promised Noah never to destroy the earth by flood, Abraham a great nation, Moses a law and a people, David a kingdom without end.
Each covenant had a sign: the rainbow, circumcision, the Law written on tablets, the throne of David (CCC 56–62). In the new covenant the signs are the sacraments, above all the Eucharist (CCC 1365).
Jesus said at the Last Supper, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The Mass makes this covenant present each time we celebrate it (CCC 762).
The idea that God changes his mind or abandons people is a common worry. Stress that God’s promises are faithful even when people fail.
talk: What promise did God make to Abraham?
What is new about the new covenant?
quiz: A covenant is…|A sacred promise-bond|A contract for money|A wish|A rule|0|CCC 56-57.
The new covenant is made in…|A city|Jesus’s blood|A temple|Moses’s law|1|Luke 22:20.
God’s covenants show that he…|Is angry|Forgets|Is far|Keeps his promises|3|CCC 62.
lessons.life: Keep one promise you made, even if it is hard.
lessons.saint: King David: a shepherd boy who became king and received a great promise.
misc: “God gets angry and breaks his promises when we sin.”
lessons.mem: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” (Luke 22:20)
lessons.hook: Shake hands, then show a wedding ring or a family photo. Ask: “What is a promise that makes people belong to each other?” Tell them God makes promises like that, and he never breaks them.
lessons.assess: Ask children to match each person (Noah, Abraham, Moses, David) with his sign and a promise.

script.open: Have two children shake hands and say a promise to each other: “I promise to share my snack.” Ask, “What makes a promise special? What if you break it?” Say, “Now think of God making a promise. It would be the biggest promise.”
teach: Say: “A covenant is a sacred promise between God and people. It is more than a contract. It makes people into God’s family. God made a series of covenants in the Old Testament, each one bigger than the one before. With Noah, God promised never to flood the earth again, and put the rainbow in the sky. With Abraham, he promised a great family and a land, and a blessing for all nations. With Moses, he gave the Law and made Israel his people. With David, he promised a king whose kingdom would last forever.”

Say: “Each time, people broke the covenant. But God did not give up. The prophet Jeremiah said that God would make a new covenant, with a law written on our hearts. Jesus fulfilled it. At the Last Supper he took the cup and said, ‘This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.’ (Luke 22:20) At Mass, we celebrate that covenant. Jesus’ sacrifice makes us God’s family.”
Say: “God keeps his promises. All the covenants lead to Jesus. And God invites us to keep our part: to love him and follow him. When we are baptized, we enter the new covenant.”
ask: What is a covenant? (A sacred promise that makes people into a family.)
Who were the people God made covenants with? (Noah, Abraham, Moses, David.)
How does Jesus make a new covenant? (By giving his Body and Blood.)
practice: Give each child a long strip of paper.
Mark five spots and label them: Noah (rainbow), Abraham (stars), Moses (tablets), David (crown), Jesus (cup and bread).
Under each, write the covenant’s promise in a sentence.
Take turns presenting the timeline to a partner.
script.close: Pray: “God, thank you for keeping your promises.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family about God’s covenants.”

tryit: Make a timeline of God’s covenants.
Draw a symbol for each.
Say what each covenant promised.
lessons.saintStory:
David was the youngest son of a man named Jesse in Bethlehem. While his big brothers went to war, David looked after sheep and played the harp. God chose him, through the prophet Samuel, to be the next king of Israel, even though he was the youngest.
He is best known for beating the giant Goliath with a sling and a stone, trusting in God. David became a great king. He wrote many psalms, songs of praise and trust. He also did wrong, but when the prophet Nathan told him about it, David was truly sorry and wrote Psalm 51, “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
God made a covenant with David, promising that one of his descendants would rule forever. That descendant is Jesus. David shows how God keeps his promises even when we fail.

units.title: The Ten Commandments
units.eq: How do we love God and others?

lessons.title: Loving God
lessons.idea: The first three commandments teach us to love God above all: worship God alone, speak his name with reverence, and keep Sunday holy. They are not rules to hold us back but the way of a loving relationship.
lessons.question: What can take God’s place in our lives?
lessons.activity: “First place” clay and prayer (25 min). Children make a small clay trophy stand with “1” on it. They list on a card things that can take God’s place (games, money, popularity) and fold it under the stand. Read Exodus 20:1–11. Practice saying “Jesus” and “God” with reverence, and plan one way to keep this Sunday holy.
teach: The first commandment: “I am the Lord your God… you shall have no other gods before me” (CCC 2084–2094). We give God our faith, hope, love and worship, and we reject idols. An idol is anything we put before God.
The second commandment: we honor God’s name (CCC 2142–2149). We do not curse or swear carelessly. We bless God’s name in the Sign of the Cross and the Our Father.
The third commandment: keep holy the Lord’s Day (CCC 2168–2176). Sunday is the day of the Resurrection, so we go to Mass and rest from unnecessary work (CCC 2177–2185).
Children often hear “commandments” as a list of no’s. Frame them as a love letter from a Father who knows what keeps us free and happy (CCC 2060–2063).
talk: What can take God’s place in our hearts?
How do we keep Sunday special?
When do we say God’s name with respect?
quiz: The first commandment says…|God first|Self first|Friends first|Money first|0|CCC 2083.
To keep the Lord’s day holy, we…|Work|Go to Mass and rest|Play only|Shop|1|CCC 2177.
God’s name should be…|Honored|Joked about|Hidden|Forgotten|0|CCC 2142.
lessons.life: Plan a screen-free hour on Sunday with your family.
lessons.saint: Polycarp: a bishop who would not put anyone or anything before God.
misc: “Using God’s name when I’m surprised is harmless.”
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” (Deuteronomy 6:5)
lessons.hook: Ask who is the most important person in your life, then who comes second. Ask: “What would happen if something else took first place, like a video game?” Put a sign saying “GOD” on the table and ask children to add things they might put in first place.
lessons.assess: Each child says one thing they will put first, one way to respect God’s name, and one way to keep Sunday special.

script.open: Hold up a toy on a pedestal, such as a cup, and say, “This is first place. Who is the most important person in the world to you? Who would be in first place in your life? Let’s find out where God is.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:1-11 slowly. Say: “Notice how the commandments begin: ‘I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of slavery.’ God first reminds the people that he loves them and has saved them. The commandments are not rules to hold us back. They are a way of loving God back. They are like the rules for a friendship.”

Say: “Commandment 1: ‘You shall have no other gods before me.’ We worship God alone. A false god is anything that we put before God, like money, a game, popularity or our own wishes. Commandment 2: ‘You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.’ God’s name is holy. We say it with love, not casually and not in anger. Jesus’ name is the same: it is a prayer. Commandment 3: ‘Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.’ For Christians, Sunday is the Lord’s Day, the day of Jesus’ Resurrection. We go to Mass, rest, and spend time with family.”

Say: “God does not need our worship. We need it. We are made to love him. Keeping God first makes everything else fall into place. It is like putting the biggest rocks into a jar first: everything else fits around them.”
ask: What does the first commandment ask? (Worship God alone, keep him first.)
What are some things that could crowd God out? (Screens, sports, stuff, being busy.)
Why do we keep Sunday holy? (It is the Lord’s Day, and we need time with God.)
practice: Give each child modeling clay. Say: “Make a little stand with a number 1 on top.”
On an index card, list three things that could take God’s first place (video games, being popular, sports, sleep-in on Sunday).
Beside each, write one way to keep God first (“pray before the game,” “go to Mass first”).
Put the stand and card together and take them home as a reminder.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you are first. Help me love you above all things.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Put your clay stand where you will see it.”

tryit: Build a “first place” stand for God.
List the things that can crowd God out.
Choose how to keep God first.
lessons.saintStory:
Polycarp was bishop of the city of Smyrna (now in Turkey) around the year 155. As a young man he had learned about Jesus from Saint John the apostle, so he knew someone who knew Jesus.
When he was eighty-six years old, the Roman authorities arrested him. They told him that if he would curse Christ and say “Caesar is Lord,” they would let him go. Polycarp answered, “Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?” He was put to death for his faith.
The Christians of Smyrna wrote a letter about him. Polycarp lived the first commandment: no one and nothing is more important than God. He also shows that old and young can be brave.

lessons.title: Loving our neighbor
lessons.idea: The other seven commandments show how to love our neighbor: honor parents, respect life, be faithful and pure, be honest and fair, and be generous and content. Jesus summed them up in one word: love.
lessons.question: Which commandment helps most at school?
lessons.activity: “Commandment charades” (25 min). Write commandments 4 to 10 on cards in kid language (obey and honor; do not hurt; be faithful and kind with your body; do not steal; tell the truth; do not be jealous; be happy with what you have). In teams, act out the right choice for a school situation while others guess the commandment. Finish with each child writing one “love action” for the week.
teach: The fourth commandment: honor your father and mother (CCC 2196–2257 treats the whole law of love of neighbor; 2214–2220 treats honoring parents). Honor includes obedience, gratitude and care.
The fifth: do not kill (CCC 2258–2330). Every human life is sacred from beginning to natural end, so we do not hurt others, and we care for our own health.
The sixth to tenth: be faithful and pure (CCC 2331–2400), do not steal (CCC 2401–2463), do not lie (CCC 2464–2513), and do not envy (CCC 2514–2557). Use child-friendly examples.
Jesus gave a summary: love God and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40; CCC 2055). Every commandment is a way to love.
quiz: Commandments 4–10 teach love of…|Self only|Neighbor|Animals|God only|1|CCC 2196.
Do not steal means…|Run|Respect others’ things|Hide|Eat|1|CCC 2401.
Honor your father and mother includes…|Laziness|Silence|Fear|Respect and obedience|3|CCC 2214.
lessons.life: Choose one commandment to focus on this week.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth Ann Seton: a wife, mother, widow and founder of schools who loved her neighbor.
misc: “I only need to follow the commandments that are easy.”
lessons.mem: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” (Mark 12:31)
lessons.hook: Act out two scenes: a child shares a snack and another grabs one. Ask which is love. Then ask: “If we had to make rules for love, what would they be?” Show that the commandments are God’s answer.
lessons.assess: Give each child a situation (a friend is left out; you found money) and ask which commandment helps and what they would do.

script.open: Show a sign with the words, “Love God. Love your neighbor.” Ask, “Which is first? Which one is second? Are they connected? Jesus said they are the two most important commandments, and the other seven commandments teach us how to do the second.”
teach: Say: “The Ten Commandments are on two tablets. The first three are about loving God. Commandments 4 to 10 are about loving our neighbor. Commandment 4: ‘Honor your father and mother.’ We respect and obey our parents, and care for them when they are old. Commandment 5: ‘You shall not kill.’ Life is a gift from God, so we never harm anyone. Commandment 6 and 9: faithfulness and purity. God made our bodies good, and we treat them, and others’ bodies, with respect.”

Say: “Commandment 7: ‘You shall not steal.’ We do not take what is not ours. We share what we have. Commandment 8: ‘You shall not bear false witness.’ We tell the truth and we don’t gossip. Commandment 10: ‘You shall not covet.’ We do not envy what other people have. We are grateful for what God has given us.”

Say: “Jesus summed up the commandments in one word: love. He said, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ (Matthew 22:39) And he said, ‘If you love me, you will keep my commandments.’ The commandments show us what love looks like.”
ask: Which commandments are about our neighbor? (Four through ten.)
How does ‘Do not steal’ show love? (We respect what belongs to others.)
What one word sums up the commandments? (Love.)
practice: Write commandments 4 to 10 on cards in kid language: “Obey and honor,” “Do not hurt,” “Be faithful and pure,” “Do not take what is not yours,” “Do not lie,” “Be pure of heart,” “Do not envy.”
Split into two teams. A child from each team draws a card and acts it out silently, without words.
The team guesses the commandment, and then tells one way it shows love.
Switch actors.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, teach us to love our neighbor.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Show love to someone using one of the commandments.”

tryit: Act out a commandment in your own words.
Guess which one the other team is acting.
Say how it shows love.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth Bayley was born in New York in 1774, and she grew up in the Episcopal Church. She married William Seton, a wealthy merchant, and they had five children. Then William’s business failed, and he became very sick. The family sailed to Italy hoping to cure him, but he died there.
In Italy Elizabeth saw how Catholics prayed, and she came to believe in the Eucharist. Back in America she became Catholic, which cost her many friends. She had to support her children, so she opened a school for girls in Baltimore, and then started a community of sisters. She started the first Catholic girls’ school in the United States.
Elizabeth Ann Seton cared for her children and her pupils, for the poor and for the sick. She lived out the commandments to love our neighbor. She was the first native-born American saint.

lessons.title: Following with a good conscience
lessons.idea: Conscience is the voice inside us that helps us know right from wrong. It must be trained, like a muscle, by prayer, the Bible, the teaching of the Church and the advice of good people. We always follow our conscience, and we always work to form it well.
lessons.question: How can you form a good conscience?
lessons.activity: “Compass check” (20 min). Present three situations (a cashier gives extra change; a friend asks you to cheat; a classmate is teased). For each, children stand at one of four corners: Pray, Read what the Church teaches, Ask a wise person, Think about the effects. Discuss why each tool helps. Then each child writes “One person I can ask when I am unsure is…”.
teach: Conscience is a judgment of reason that tells us the moral quality of an act (CCC 1776–1778). “Deep within his conscience man discovers a law which he has not laid upon himself” (CCC 1776).
We must always obey our conscience, and we must form it (CCC 1783–1785). We form it by listening to God’s word, praying, asking for advice, and examining our actions each day.
Romans 2:15 says the law is written on our hearts. Even people who have not heard the Gospel have a conscience. The Holy Spirit helps us hear it clearly.
Do not confuse conscience with feelings. A person can feel fine about a wrong choice. That is why we learn what is true.
talk: How do you know when something is wrong?
Who helps you form your conscience?
What do you do when you’re unsure?
quiz: Conscience is…|A rule|A judgment of reason about right and wrong|A feeling|A habit|1|CCC 1778.
We form conscience by…|Following friends|Prayer, learning and advice|Ignoring it|Guessing|1|CCC 1785.
We should always follow…|Whim|Peers|Fear|A well-formed conscience|3|CCC 1790.
lessons.life: When in doubt this week, ask a parent or teacher before deciding.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: a lawyer who would not go against his conscience.
misc: “My conscience is just what I feel like.”
“If nobody sees me, it doesn’t matter.”
lessons.mem: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love.
lessons.hook: Show two compasses: one that works and one that is bent. Ask which you would trust to find the way home. Explain that conscience is like a compass; it must be set by God’s truth.
lessons.assess: Present a new situation and ask which tools of conscience they would use, and why.

script.open: Hold up a compass and say, “What does a compass do? It points north, no matter where you are. Do we have anything like that inside us? There is something that points us toward what is good.” Let children guess before naming it.
teach: Say: “It is called conscience. Conscience is the voice in our heart that helps us know right from wrong. It tells us, ‘Do this. Avoid that.’ When we do something good, we feel peace. When we do something wrong, we feel uneasy. God put this voice in our hearts. Romans 2:15 says God’s law is written on our hearts.”

Say: “But conscience, like a compass, can be off if it is not looked after. Our conscience needs to be trained. We train it by praying, learning the Bible and the Ten Commandments, listening to the Church, and asking advice from wise people, like parents and teachers. A conscience can be wrong if we don’t know the truth.”

Say: “Two rules: First, we always follow our conscience. It is wrong to do what we think is wrong. Second, we always work to form it well, by learning what is true and good. And if we are not sure, we ask someone who knows. If we sin, we can go to Confession.”
ask: What is conscience? (The inner voice that helps us know right from wrong.)
How do we train our conscience? (Prayer, the Bible, the Church, good advice.)
What do we do if we aren’t sure? (Ask a wise person.)
practice: Present three situations one at a time: a cashier gives you extra change; a friend asks you to cheat on a test; a classmate is being teased.
After each, give the children a minute to think. Pair them to discuss using three questions: “Is it kind? Is it true? What would Jesus do?”
Take answers. Talk about what makes it hard.
Pray the “Come, Holy Spirit” prayer for help in making choices.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “When you must choose this week, ask the three questions.”

tryit: Work through the three situations.
Ask: Is it kind? True? Would Jesus do it?
Say what you would do.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas More was born in London in 1478. He became a lawyer and was famous for his wit and wisdom. He married and had four children and spent time with them every day. He also became an adviser to King Henry VIII and was made Lord Chancellor of England, the highest position in the land.
When King Henry decided to break from the Pope and make himself head of the Church in England, he demanded that everyone take an oath agreeing with this. Thomas could not do it in good conscience. He remained silent, but he would not take the oath. He was put in prison in the Tower of London for over a year, and then executed in 1535.
His last words were reported to be that he died “the king’s good servant, but God’s first.” Thomas More teaches us to follow our conscience, formed by the truth.

lessons.title: The Beatitudes
lessons.idea: The Beatitudes are Jesus’ eight surprising promises of happiness. They describe the life of a disciple and point toward heaven: blessed are the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, the hungry for justice, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted.
lessons.question: Which Beatitude is most surprising?
lessons.activity: “Beatitude picture book” (30 min). In pairs, each takes one Beatitude, restates it in child words, draws a scene showing someone living it, and names a real person (a saint, a family member) who is like that. Bind the pages as a class book and read it aloud at the end.
teach: The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12) are the heart of Jesus’ preaching (CCC 1716). They describe Christ’s own life and the path to heaven, and answer our desire for happiness.
“Blessed” means truly happy. The Beatitudes show that real happiness comes from God and from loving others, not from having more (CCC 1718–1719, 1725).

Let children match a saint to each: Francis of Assisi (poor in spirit), Teresa of Calcutta (merciful), Maria Goretti (pure in heart), John XXIII (peacemaker), Thomas More (persecuted for righteousness).
The last Beatitude, persecution, may frighten children. Say that being a friend of Jesus is sometimes hard, and that he promises to be with us.
quiz: The Beatitudes are from…|Genesis|Acts|The Sermon on the Mount|Revelation|2|Matthew 5.
Blessed are the…|Poor in spirit|Famous|Rich|Strong|0|Matthew 5:3.
The Beatitudes point to…|Wealth|True happiness|Fame|Power|1|CCC 1721.
lessons.life: Do something for “the meek” or “the peacemakers” this week.
lessons.saint: Pier Giorgio Frassati: a joyful young man who lived the Beatitudes in the mountains and among the poor.
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do people say makes you happy?” (stuff, winning, being popular). Then read Matthew 5:3 aloud: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Ask: “Does that sound like what the world says?” Let them wonder.
lessons.assess: Each child chooses one Beatitude, says it in their own words and names one action to live it this week.

script.open: Ask the children, “If you could have anything to make you really happy, what would it be?” Write the answers on the board. “Now listen to what Jesus said would make us happy. It might surprise you.”
teach: Read Matthew 5:3-12 slowly. Say: “Jesus sat on a mountain and taught his disciples. He gave eight promises of happiness. The word Beatitude comes from the Latin for ‘blessed.’ Each begins ‘Blessed are…’ and ends with a promise.”

Go through them in kid words: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: those who know they need God. Blessed are those who mourn: God comforts them. Blessed are the meek: the gentle will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: they will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful: they will receive mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart: they will see God. Blessed are the peacemakers: they will be called children of God. Blessed are those who are persecuted for doing right: the kingdom of heaven is theirs.”

Say: “These surprise us. The world says: be rich, be strong, get even. Jesus says: be humble, be gentle, forgive. The Beatitudes are a picture of Jesus himself, and the way of a disciple. And they lead to heaven. Jesus lived every one of them.”
ask: What does ‘blessed’ mean? (Happy, favored by God.)
Which Beatitude is the hardest for you? Why? (Take answers.)
How are the Beatitudes different from what the world says? (They reverse it: humble, gentle, merciful.)
practice: Assign each pair one Beatitude. Have them restate it in kid words.
Each pair draws a scene of someone living it, such as a child comforting a friend who is sad.
Write the Beatitude and a caption.
Compile the pages into a class book, and read it aloud.
script.close: Read the Beatitudes one more time with a reader for each. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose one Beatitude to live this week.”

tryit: Pick one Beatitude.
Say it in your own words.
Draw someone living it.
lessons.saintStory:
Pier Giorgio Frassati was born in Turin, Italy, in 1901, to a wealthy family. His father owned a newspaper. Pier Giorgio had everything he needed, but he was not interested in showing off. He loved the mountains, and he went hiking and climbing with his friends, praying the Rosary on the way. His motto was “Verso l’alto,” or “To the heights.”
He also loved the poor. He visited poor families in the slums of Turin, bringing food and helping them, and often gave away his own bus fare and had to run home. He did this quietly, and his family did not know how much until his funeral, when huge crowds of poor people came.
Pier Giorgio died of polio at twenty-four, in 1925. He was named a saint in 2025. He lived the Beatitudes: merciful, pure of heart, and a peacemaker.

lessons.title: Faith, hope and love
lessons.idea: Faith, hope and love are the theological virtues. God gives them to us at Baptism so we can believe in him, trust his promises and love him and others as he loves us. The greatest is love.
lessons.question: How can we grow in virtue?
lessons.activity: “Virtue chain” (25 min). Provide paper links in three colors. For each virtue, children write an action that shows it at home, at school, at church. Link the chain around the room. Discuss: how do we grow in a virtue? (practice, prayer, sacraments).
teach: Theological virtues come directly from God and lead to God (CCC 1812–1813). They are given at Baptism and grow through prayer and the sacraments.

Faith is believing God and all he has revealed (CCC 1814). Hope is trusting his promises and desiring heaven (CCC 1817). Charity, or love, is loving God above all and neighbor as ourselves (CCC 1822).
1 Corinthians 13:13: “faith, hope and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.” Love is greatest because it lasts forever (CCC 1826).
Virtues are habits: we get better with practice. Connect to sports or music so children see the pattern.
talk: How can you love a difficult person?
quiz: The three theological virtues are…|Joy, peace, patience|Courage, fairness, wisdom|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving|Faith, hope, love|3|CCC 1812.
The greatest is…|Faith|Courage|Hope|Love|3|1 Corinthians 13:13.
Virtues are…|Rules|Good habits|Games|Gifts only|1|CCC 1803.
lessons.life: Practice one virtue each day: faith on Monday, hope on Tuesday, love on Wednesday.
lessons.saint: Vincent de Paul: a priest whose faith, hope and love turned into action for the poor.
lessons.mem: “Faith, hope and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.” (1 Corinthians 13:13)
lessons.hook: Show three gifts in a box labeled Faith, Hope, Love. Ask what each might hold. Open them: a pair of glasses (faith sees what we cannot), an anchor (hope holds), a heart (love gives).
lessons.assess: Ask each child to give a situation where they could show faith, one for hope and one for love.

script.open: Give each child a piece of paper with three words: faith, hope, love. Ask, “Which one is easiest for you? Which is the hardest?” Let them mark it and share with a partner.
teach: Say: “At your Baptism, God gave you three special gifts called theological virtues, because they come from God and lead to God. They are faith, hope and love. Faith means believing in God and everything he has told us, even when we cannot see. Hope means trusting God’s promises, especially that he will bring us to heaven. Love, also called charity, means loving God above all, and loving others as God loves us.”

Read 1 Corinthians 13:13: “So faith, hope and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.” Say: “Paul says love is the greatest. That is because in heaven, we won’t need faith (we will see God), and we won’t need hope (we will have it), but love goes on forever. God is love.”

Say: “These virtues are like muscles that grow when we use them. We practice faith when we pray and trust God. We practice hope when we do not give up. We practice love when we help someone, forgive and share. God gives us the gifts, and we say yes by acting.”
ask: What are the three theological virtues? (Faith, hope and love.)
Which is the greatest? (Love.)
How can we practice hope? (Trust God, don’t give up.)
practice: Cut paper strips in three colors, one for each virtue.
Each child writes one action on each color: faith (“pray before a test”), hope (“keep trying when it’s hard”), love (“include someone who is alone”).
Make links and join them in a class chain, color by color.
Hang the chain and choose one link to try this week.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, increase my faith, my hope and my love.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose one link from the chain and do it.”

tryit: Write an action for faith, hope and love.
Add it to the chain.
Choose one to do this week.
lessons.saintStory:
Vincent was born in France in 1581, and grew up on a farm. He became a priest, and at first he wanted a comfortable life. But as a priest he saw how hard life was for the poor: hungry families, sick people with no care, and prisoners chained to the oars of galleys.
Vincent changed his heart. He collected food and money for the poor. He started groups of volunteers to visit the sick, and with Louise de Marillac, began the Daughters of Charity, sisters who served the poor in the streets. He founded priests to teach and serve the poor in the countryside. He is said to have told his helpers that the poor are our “lords and masters.”
Vincent shows faith in action: trusting that Christ is in the poor, hoping that things can change, and loving through deeds.

lessons.title: Courage, fairness, wisdom, self-control
lessons.idea: The four cardinal virtues are prudence (choosing wisely), justice (giving others what they deserve), fortitude (being brave) and temperance (self-control). They are the “hinges” of a good life, and with God’s help they become habits.
lessons.question: What helps you control your temper?
lessons.activity: “Four hinges” relay (25 min). Four stations, one per virtue, each with a scenario card (e.g., “You see a younger child being teased”). At each, a team decides what the virtue looks like and acts it out. Then everyone writes a personal goal: “I will practice [virtue] by…”.
teach: Prudence helps us see what is good and choose the right way (CCC 1806). Justice gives God and neighbor what is due (CCC 1807). Fortitude gives courage in difficulty (CCC 1808). Temperance moderates our desires (CCC 1809).
Wisdom 8:7 says that wisdom teaches “self-control and prudence, justice and courage.” These virtues were known to the Greeks and then deepened by Christ (CCC 1805).
Virtues are built by repeated good acts and by grace. Saints like Thomas More (justice), Joan of Arc (fortitude) and Francis de Sales (gentleness) can be stories.
Children may think virtues are about being perfect. Stress that we grow bit by bit, and that mistakes are chances to try again.
talk: How do you control your temper?
quiz: Prudence is…|Being quiet|Being strong|Choosing well|Being fair|2|CCC 1806.
Justice gives…|Candy|Chores|Rest|What is due|3|CCC 1807.
Temperance helps with…|Self-control|Reading|Running|Singing|0|CCC 1809.
lessons.life: Practice temperance by waiting patiently in line.
lessons.saint: Louis IX of France: a king who tried to be fair, brave and self-controlled.
lessons.mem: “Be strong and of good courage… for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.” (Joshua 1:9)
lessons.hook: Show a door and its hinge. Explain that “cardinal” comes from the Latin for hinge: these four virtues are like hinges on which a good life swings. Open and close the door several times.
lessons.assess: Give scenarios and ask which virtue each calls for.

script.open: Open a door and let it swing on its hinges. Say, “What does a hinge do? Without it, the door is useless. There are four ‘hinge’ virtues, too, because the rest of a good life swings on them.”
teach: Say: “The word ‘cardinal’ comes from the Latin word for ‘hinge.’ The four cardinal virtues are the hinges of a good life. They are habits, things we get good at by practicing, and God helps us. The first is prudence. Prudence means choosing wisely. Before we act, we think about what is good and the best way to do it. Wisdom 8:7 says wisdom teaches temperance, prudence, justice and fortitude.”

Say: “The second is justice. Justice means giving everyone what they deserve: fairness, respect, and what is owed. We share, we tell the truth, we keep promises. The third is fortitude, which means courage. It is the strength to do what is right even when it is hard or scary. The fourth is temperance, which means self-control. We use good things in the right amount. We don’t eat too much, watch too much or want everything.”

Say: “Virtues are habits, like practicing a sport. The more we practice, the easier it gets. We build them by choosing good again and again. And with God’s grace they become part of us. We pray: ‘God, help me be wise, fair, brave and self-controlled.’”
ask: What are the four cardinal virtues? (Prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance.)
Which one helps you resist too much screen time? (Temperance.)
When is it hard to be brave? (Take answers: standing up for someone, telling the truth.)
practice: Set up four stations, one per virtue, each with a situation card. For example: Prudence: you must decide what to do after school; Justice: two children want the same toy; Fortitude: a younger child is being teased; Temperance: you have a plate of cookies.
Groups visit each station for four minutes, discuss and decide what to do, and write or act it.
After the rotation, discuss which was the hardest.
Close with a one-sentence goal for each virtue.
script.close: Pray: “God, make me wise, fair, brave and self-controlled.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Practice one virtue this week.”

tryit: Go to each of the four stations.
Solve the problem using the virtue.
Say how it takes courage or self-control.
lessons.saintStory:
Louis IX was born in 1214, and became king of France at twelve. His mother, Blanche of Castile, ruled for him until he was older, and she taught him that she would rather see him dead than commit a mortal sin.
Louis tried to rule justly. He is remembered for sitting under an oak tree at Vincennes, listening to anyone who had a complaint, rich or poor. He set up courts to make justice fair, and ended unfair practices. He fasted, prayed the Hours, and gave to the poor. He fed beggars at his own table and washed the feet of the poor. He also went on two Crusades, was captured once, and died of illness in Tunis in 1270.
Louis shows the four cardinal virtues: wisdom in choosing, justice in treating others fairly, courage in danger and self-control in living simply.

units.title: Jesus the Savior
units.eq: Who is Jesus and what did he do?

lessons.title: Jesus is true God and true man
lessons.idea: Jesus is true God and true man. The eternal Son of God became a human being, was born of Mary, and lived among us. He did this to save us and to show us the Father.
lessons.question: What shows that Jesus is human? That he is God?
lessons.activity: “Two columns” poster (25 min). Children make a poster with two columns: “Jesus is human” (hungry, tired, cried, had a mother) and “Jesus is God” (forgave sins, calmed storms, rose from the dead). Each child adds evidence from a Gospel story assigned to them: Mark 4:35–41, John 11:35, Luke 7:48.
teach: The Incarnation: God’s Son became man (CCC 461–463). He remained God and took a human nature, so he is one Person with two natures (CCC 464–469).
Jesus experienced hunger, tiredness, joy and sorrow (CCC 470–478). He also forgave sins and commanded storms, showing he is God.
Why did he become man? To save us, to show God’s love, to be our model of holiness, and to make us sharers in God’s life (CCC 457–460).
Avoid either error: that Jesus only seemed human, or that he was just a good man. Use plain words.
quiz: Jesus is…|Only man|Only God|True God and true man|An angel|2|CCC 464.
The Incarnation means…|God became man|A story|A trick|Man became God|0|CCC 461.
Jesus got…|Tired and hungry|Never tired|Lost|Sick of God|0|CCC 470.
lessons.life: Pray, “Jesus, true God and true man, have mercy on me.”
lessons.saint: Athanasius: he defended the truth about Jesus.
misc: “Jesus was only pretending to be human.”
“Jesus was a good teacher, but not God.”
lessons.mem: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” (John 1:14)
lessons.hook: Hold two objects: a toy knight’s crown and a plain cloak. Say: “Imagine a king who puts on a servant’s clothes to live among his people.” Then read John 1:14. Jesus did something even greater.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Name one thing that shows Jesus is human and one that shows he is God.”

script.open: Hold up a picture of a baby, and then a picture of a king on a throne. Ask, “Can one person be both? That’s the amazing news about Jesus.”
teach: Read John 1:1,14: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Say: “The Word is God’s Son, who always existed with the Father. At a point in time, he became a human being, in the womb of Mary. This is called the Incarnation: ‘in the flesh.’ Christmas celebrates it.”

Say: “Jesus is true God and true man. He is fully God. He is the second Person of the Trinity. He has no beginning. He has the power to heal and forgive sins. And he is fully human. He had a body. He was born, grew tired, was hungry, got angry, cried at his friend’s grave, and died. He had a human mind and heart. He is exactly like us, except without sin.”

Say: “Why did God become a man? To save us, to show us how much the Father loves us, and to show us how to live. Only someone who is both God and man can bring us back to God. A bridge needs to touch both sides of the river. Jesus is the bridge between God and us.”
ask: What does ‘Incarnation’ mean? (God the Son became flesh, a human being.)
Give an example showing that Jesus is human. (He was hungry, tired, cried.)
Give an example showing he is God. (He forgave sins, calmed the storm, rose from the dead.)
practice: Give each child a sheet of paper divided into two columns.
Head them “Jesus is human” and “Jesus is God.” Brainstorm: for human, hungry, tired, wept, had a mother; for God, forgave sins, raised the dead, calmed the storm.
Add Gospel references, such as Luke 8:24 (asleep in the boat) and Mark 4:39 (calms the storm).
Draw a symbol at the top: a manger and a crown.
script.close: Say: “Jesus, you are true God and true man. We praise you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell someone why Jesus became a man.”

tryit: Make a two-column poster.
On one side: Jesus is human.
On the other: Jesus is God.
lessons.saintStory:
Athanasius was born around the year 296 in Alexandria, Egypt. As a young deacon he attended the Council of Nicaea in 325, where bishops from all over the Church met to answer a question: Is Jesus truly God? A priest named Arius said that Jesus was a creature, made by God, not equal with the Father. The Council said no: Jesus is truly God, “of one substance” with the Father.
Athanasius spent the rest of his life defending this truth. When he became bishop of Alexandria, powerful people who believed Arius was right had him sent away. He was exiled five times, and spent about seventeen years away from his people, but he did not give up. People said it was “Athanasius against the world.”
He wrote a book called On the Incarnation, which says that God became a human being so that we could share in God’s life. Athanasius shows how much it matters that Jesus is both God and man.

lessons.title: Jesus teaches and heals
lessons.idea: Jesus announced that God’s kingdom had come, and he showed it by teaching and by miracles. His miracles are signs that point to who he is and call us to trust him.
lessons.question: Why did Jesus do miracles?
lessons.activity: “Sign or magic?” sort (20 min). Provide cards of Gospel miracles (calming the storm, feeding five thousand, healing the blind man, raising Jairus’ daughter). For each, children write what it shows about Jesus (power over nature, compassion, power over death) and what it asks of us (trust). Then compare with magic tricks: what is different?
teach: Jesus preached the Kingdom of God with parables and with actions (CCC 541–546). Miracles were “works of God” that showed the Kingdom had come (CCC 547–550).
Miracles are signs. They invite faith; they do not force it (CCC 548). Jesus did not use miracles to show off but to heal and free (CCC 549).
Jesus’ biggest sign is his Resurrection. Healing and forgiveness connect: he healed bodies as a sign of healing souls (Mark 2:1–12).
Children may ask why Jesus doesn’t heal everyone today. Answer honestly: God cares, he works in many ways, and he asks us to be his hands.
talk: How do miracles help us believe?
quiz: Miracles are…|Tricks|Signs of God’s power|Magic|Accidents|1|CCC 547.
Jesus calmed…|A storm|A road|A house|A tree|0|Mark 4:39.
He raised…|Lazarus|A king|A coin|A tree|0|John 11.
lessons.life: Thank God for a “small miracle” each day.
lessons.saint: Luke the Evangelist: a physician who wrote about Jesus’ healings.
misc: “If I pray hard enough, God must do what I ask.”
lessons.mem: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41)
lessons.hook: Read the first lines of Mark 4:35–41, then stop at the storm. Ask what they would do. Then read the end: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name one miracle, what it shows about Jesus, and how we should respond.

script.open: Say, “Imagine you are in a boat on a lake, and a huge storm comes. The waves are crashing in. The boat is filling with water. And Jesus is asleep in the back. What would you do?” Let children respond. Then read what the disciples did.
teach: Read Mark 4:35-41 aloud. Say: “The disciples were afraid and woke him up: ‘Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?’ Jesus stood up, and said to the wind, ‘Peace! Be still!’ And the wind stopped, and it was completely calm. Then he asked, ‘Why are you afraid? Have you no faith?’ And they asked each other, ‘Who is this, that even the wind and sea obey him?’”

Say: “Jesus did many miracles. He healed the sick, made the blind see, fed five thousand people, and raised the dead. In Luke 8:40-56 he raises the daughter of Jairus, saying, ‘Little girl, arise!’ But miracles are not magic tricks. They are signs. A sign points to something. The miracles of Jesus point to who he is: the Son of God with power over nature, sickness and death. They show that God’s kingdom has come.”

Say: “The miracles also show Jesus’ compassion. He healed because he loved people. And they call us to faith. Many people believed in Jesus because of his miracles. Jesus still works through the sacraments, such as the Anointing of the Sick, and in answer to prayer.”
ask: What is a sign? (Something that points to something else.)
What did the calming of the storm show about Jesus? (He has power over nature, he is God.)
Why did Jesus work miracles? (Compassion, to show who he is, to call us to faith.)
practice: Prepare cards of Gospel miracles: calming the storm, feeding five thousand, healing the blind man, raising Jairus’s daughter, walking on water, the wedding at Cana.
Prepare two headings: “A sign about who Jesus is” and “Magic trick.” Sort the cards (all go under signs!).
For each, write: “This shows Jesus is…”
Choose one miracle and retell it to a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, we believe in you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the story of a miracle with your family.”

tryit: Sort the miracle cards.
Say what each one shows about Jesus.
Choose one to retell.
lessons.saintStory:
Luke was a Greek doctor, and a friend and companion of Saint Paul. He was not one of the twelve apostles, and he never met Jesus during his life on earth. But he carefully collected the stories of those who did, as he says at the start of his Gospel: “I decided to write an orderly account for you.”
Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. His Gospel has stories that are not found in the others: the Annunciation, the shepherds, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son. He pays attention to the poor, women, and sinners, and to Jesus’ mercy. He had a doctor’s eye for the details of healing.
Tradition says that Luke was a painter, too, and that he painted a picture of Mary. He is the patron of doctors and artists. He shows us Jesus the healer.

lessons.title: Cross and Resurrection
lessons.idea: Jesus died on the cross to forgive our sins and rose from the dead on the third day. His Resurrection shows he is God, defeats death, and opens heaven to us. Easter is the greatest feast.
lessons.question: Why is Easter the biggest feast?
lessons.activity: “Three days” storyboard (25 min). Fold a paper into three: Friday (the Cross), Saturday (the tomb), Sunday (the empty tomb). Children draw each scene and write one sentence. Read Luke 23:33–46 and 24:1–12 in pieces. End with a joyful “Alleluia!” as they unveil the Sunday panel.
teach: Jesus died “for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3; CCC 599–605). His death was a free gift of love (CCC 609–614).
On the third day he rose in his glorified body (CCC 638–644). He ate with his disciples, and they touched him. The empty tomb and his appearances are the foundation of our faith.
The Resurrection means death is not the end, sin is forgiven and heaven is open (CCC 651–655). Every Sunday is a “little Easter.”
Be gentle with Good Friday. Children can be upset by the Cross. Emphasize love and the victory of Easter.
quiz: Jesus died on…|A bed|A hill of stone|A boat|The cross|3|CCC 613.
On the third day he…|Left|Stayed dead|Hid|Rose|3|CCC 638.
The Resurrection shows…|It was a story|Jesus conquered death|He was tricked|It was a dream|1|CCC 654.
lessons.life: Make a cross from two sticks and place it in your home.
lessons.saint: Joseph of Arimathea: a disciple who buried Jesus with honor.
misc: “Easter is mostly about bunnies and eggs.”
lessons.mem: “He is not here; he has risen!” (Luke 24:6)
lessons.hook: Show a seed in dry dirt. Say: “It looks dead, but watch.” Show a picture of a plant. Read John 12:24 (“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies…”). Say, “Jesus is the seed that gives life.”
lessons.assess: Have children retell the story in order and tell why Easter is joyful.

script.open: Have the room very quiet. Say, “I am going to tell you the most important three days in the history of the world. They happened a very long time ago. Friday. Saturday. Sunday.”
teach: Read Luke 23:33-46 in pieces. Say: “On Friday, Jesus was crucified. He was nailed to a cross between two criminals. He prayed, ‘Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.’ He told the good thief, ‘Today you will be with me in paradise.’ At about three o’clock he cried out, ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.’ And he died. It was the darkest day. Jesus did this out of love, to forgive our sins.”
Say: “On Saturday his body lay in the tomb. His friends were sad and afraid, and the Sabbath was a day of rest. It was quiet. It seemed that all was lost.”

Read Luke 24:1-12. Say: “Then, on Sunday morning, early, some women went to the tomb with spices. The stone had been rolled away. The tomb was empty! Two men in shining clothes said, ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen.’ Jesus rose from the dead on the third day! The Resurrection shows that Jesus is God, that death is not the end, and that heaven is open to us. Easter is the greatest feast of the year.”
ask: Why did Jesus die on the cross? (To forgive our sins and save us.)
What happened on the third day? (He rose from the dead.)
What does the Resurrection prove? (Jesus is God, he defeated death, and heaven is open.)
practice: Give each child a paper to fold into three columns.
Label them: Friday: The Cross; Saturday: The Tomb; Sunday: The Empty Tomb.
In each, draw a scene and write a sentence.
Partner up and retell the three days. End by saying together: “He is risen!”
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, you died for us and rose for us. Thank you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family the story of the three days.”

tryit: Fold your paper in three.
Draw Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
Tell the story to a partner.
lessons.saintStory:
Joseph came from the town of Arimathea and was a rich man and a member of the Jewish council. The Gospels say that he was a good and righteous man who was waiting for the kingdom of God, and a secret disciple of Jesus, because he was afraid of what others would say.
On Friday afternoon, after Jesus had died, most of the disciples were hiding. But Joseph bravely went to Pilate, the Roman governor, and asked for Jesus’ body. With Nicodemus, another man who had come to Jesus at night, he took the body down from the cross, wrapped it in clean linen with spices, and laid it in his own new tomb, which was cut in the rock. Then they rolled a stone across the entrance.
Joseph’s courage showed his love. No one was willing, and he stepped up. He shows what to do when it is hard to stand up for Jesus.

units.title: The Holy Spirit and the Church
units.eq: What does the Holy Spirit do?

lessons.title: Pentecost
lessons.idea: On Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon Mary and the apostles like wind and fire. They were filled with courage, preached to the crowds, and the Church began. The same Spirit is given to us in Baptism and Confirmation.
lessons.question: What changed for the apostles?
lessons.activity: “Pentecost on the move” (25 min). Cut red and orange paper flames. On each flame, children write a gift they need from the Spirit (courage, wisdom, kindness). Tell Acts 2 with sounds: wind (whooshing), fire (clap), languages (greeting in different languages). Hang the flames over a picture of the Church.
teach: The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity, God like the Father and Son (CCC 685–687). At Pentecost he filled the apostles and made the Church visible to the world (CCC 731–732).
Symbols of the Spirit: wind, fire, water, oil, dove (CCC 694–701). Teach two or three that children can see in church.
Before Pentecost the apostles hid; afterward they spoke boldly. The Spirit gives courage, truth and unity.
Avoid presenting the Spirit as a force. He is a Person who loves, teaches and guides.
quiz: Pentecost took place…|On Good Friday|In Lent|At Christmas|Fifty days after Easter|3|CCC 731.
The apostles spoke…|Only Hebrew|Many languages|Only Latin|Nothing|1|Acts 2:4.
The Spirit is…|An angel|A saint|A ghost|God|3|CCC 685.
lessons.life: Pray a Veni Creator or “Come, Holy Spirit” each morning.
lessons.saint: Barnabas: a generous man whose name means “son of encouragement.”
misc: “The Holy Spirit is just a feeling.”
lessons.mem: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love.
lessons.hook: Open a window or use a small fan and a candle (safely). Say: “You can’t see wind but you can see what it does.” Light the candle. Say the Spirit is like both: strong and warm. Then read Acts 2:1–4.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What happened at Pentecost, and how does the Spirit help us today?”

script.open: Put a candle out of reach, and a lighter or an electric candle. Say, “A candle is just wax and a wick until it is lit. The disciples were like unlit candles until Pentecost. Let’s see what happened.”
teach: Tell Acts 2:1-4 with energy: “Fifty days after Easter, the disciples were gathered in a room in Jerusalem, afraid. Mary was with them. Suddenly there was a sound from heaven like a mighty wind. Something like tongues of fire appeared and rested on each of them. They were filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in other languages.”

Say: “Crowds from all over the world were in Jerusalem for the feast, and each one heard the apostles speaking in his own language. Peter stood up and preached to them boldly. He said that Jesus, who was crucified, God had made Lord and Christ. About three thousand people were baptized that day. This is the birthday of the Church.”

Say: “The same Holy Spirit is given to us. We receive him in Baptism, and in a special way in Confirmation. The Spirit gives us gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. And he gives fruits, such as love, joy, peace and patience. The Spirit makes us brave to follow Jesus, helps us pray, and makes us one in the Church.”
ask: What happened at Pentecost? (The Holy Spirit came, like wind and fire.)
What changed in the apostles? (They were brave and spoke about Jesus.)
When do we receive the Holy Spirit? (Baptism and Confirmation.)
practice: Cut flame shapes from red, orange and yellow paper.
Have each child write on a flame one gift they need from the Holy Spirit, such as courage, kindness, wisdom, patience.
Tape the flames to a big paper cross, a dove, or a wall, as a class “Pentecost fire.”
Stand in a circle and pray: “Come, Holy Spirit” after each child reads their gift.
script.close: Pray together the “Come, Holy Spirit” prayer. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask the Holy Spirit for your gift every morning.”

tryit: Write a gift you need from the Spirit on a flame.
Add it to the wall.
Pray for each other.
lessons.saintStory:
Barnabas was a Jewish man from the island of Cyprus. His real name was Joseph, but the apostles called him Barnabas, which means “son of encouragement,” because of how he cheered people up.
After Pentecost the first Christians shared everything they had. Barnabas had a field, sold it, and put the money at the apostles’ feet. When Saul, the man who had once persecuted Christians, came to Jerusalem, everyone was afraid of him. Barnabas welcomed him and introduced him to the apostles. Later, Barnabas and Saul, who became Paul, went on a mission trip together.
Barnabas shows what the Holy Spirit does: he fills us with generosity, courage and the desire to encourage others.

lessons.title: The Church is one, holy, catholic, apostolic
lessons.idea: The Church Jesus founded is one, holy, catholic and apostolic. One because she has one Lord, one faith, one Baptism; holy because Christ makes her holy; catholic because she is for everyone everywhere; apostolic because she is built on the apostles and their successors.
lessons.question: What do these four words mean?
lessons.activity: “Four marks puzzle” (25 min). Cut a church picture into four pieces labeled One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic. Children complete it by reading a clue at each piece (Ephesians 4:4–6 for One; Matthew 28:19 for Catholic; Ephesians 2:20 for Apostolic) and giving an example.
teach: The Creed names four marks of the Church (CCC 811–870). They help us recognize the Church Jesus founded.

One: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (CCC 813–815). Holy: God is holy and he makes his people holy; saints show it (CCC 823–829). Catholic means “universal”: for all people and with the fullness of the faith (CCC 830–831).
Apostolic: built on the apostles, with bishops as their successors and the Pope as successor of Peter (CCC 857–865).
Avoid suggesting other Christians are not Christians. Say we are united by Baptism, and pray for unity.
quiz: “Catholic” means…|Old|Universal|Local|Roman|1|CCC 830.
Apostolic means…|Local|Ancient|Large|Founded on the apostles|3|CCC 857.
The Church is holy because…|The building is old|Christ is holy|The priest is good|People are perfect|1|CCC 823.
lessons.life: Say the marks at Mass and think what each means.
lessons.saint: Paul: the man who persecuted the Church and then became its greatest missionary.
misc: “Holy means everyone in the Church is perfect.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.” (from the Nicene Creed)
lessons.hook: Show four photos: one family at a table (one), a stained-glass saint (holy), a world map (catholic), a line of people passing a torch (apostolic). Ask what word each might show.
lessons.assess: Give each mark and ask for its meaning and an example.

script.open: Show a picture of a very large building with four pillars. Say, “Four pillars hold up this building. The Church that Jesus founded stands on four marks too. Let’s find out what they are.”
teach: Say: “The Church Jesus founded has four marks, or special signs. We say them in the Nicene Creed on Sundays: ‘I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.’ The first mark is that the Church is one. Paul wrote, ‘There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, one God and Father of all.’ (Ephesians 4:4-6) We are one because we have one Lord, one faith and one Baptism, and one leader, the Pope.”

Say: “The second mark is holy. The Church is holy because Jesus is holy and he makes her holy, with the sacraments and his teaching. The members of the Church are sinners, but the Church herself is holy, because Christ is her head. The third mark is catholic, which means ‘universal.’ The Church is for everyone, everywhere, in all times. She has the fullness of the truth and the means of salvation.”

Say: “The fourth mark is apostolic. The Church is built on the apostles, whom Jesus chose. Their successors, the bishops, continue their work. We trace the line of bishops back to the apostles in an unbroken chain. When you go to Mass anywhere in the world, you will see the same faith, because of these marks.”
ask: What are the four marks? (One, holy, catholic, apostolic.)
What does ‘catholic’ mean? (Universal, for everyone everywhere.)
Why is the Church holy even though her members sin? (Jesus is holy, and gives her holiness.)
practice: Cut a picture of a church into four pieces labeled One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic.
Give each group a set. They put it together and, on the back of each piece, write what the mark means in their own words.
Come up with a symbol for each mark, like a hand-in-hand circle, a halo, a globe and a chain.
Share with the class.
script.close: Say the line from the Creed together: “I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Listen for the four marks in the Creed at Mass.”

tryit: Put the four-piece church puzzle together.
Write one word on each piece: One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic.
Explain each mark to a partner.
lessons.saintStory:
Saul was a young Jewish man from the city of Tarsus. He was a strict student of the law, and he thought that the followers of Jesus were wrong. He was present at the death of Stephen, the first martyr, and he went from house to house arresting Christians.
On his way to the city of Damascus, a bright light flashed from heaven, and Saul fell to the ground. A voice said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Saul was blind for three days. Then a disciple named Ananias baptized him, and he could see again. He took the name Paul.
Paul traveled by ship and on foot across the Mediterranean, preaching to Jews and Gentiles, planting churches and writing letters. He said the Church is one body, with many members. He was put to death in Rome. Paul shows how Christ can change anyone.

lessons.title: Pope, bishops, priests and laypeople
lessons.idea: The Church is a family with different members. The Pope leads the whole Church as successor of Peter, bishops lead dioceses as successors of the apostles, priests and deacons serve, and all the baptized (the laity) share Jesus’ mission in the world.
lessons.question: Who are the leaders in your diocese?
lessons.activity: “Church family tree” (25 min). Children build a chart: Jesus, Peter and the apostles, Pope, bishop of your diocese (find the name), your pastor, deacons, parents and teachers, children. Under each, write what they do (teach, lead, celebrate sacraments, serve). Add “my part is…”.
teach: Christ is the head and the Church is his Body (CCC 791–795). The Pope, bishop of Rome, is the successor of St Peter and has care for the whole Church (CCC 880–882).
Bishops teach, sanctify and govern; priests help the bishop and celebrate Mass and sacraments; deacons serve at the altar, the Word and charity (CCC 874–896).
The laity make up most of the Church and share in Christ’s mission to be priest, prophet and king in daily life (CCC 897–913).
Name your bishop and pastor. Children love knowing real names.
quiz: The Pope is…|A king|A prophet|An emperor|Successor of Peter|3|CCC 882.
The laity are…|Baptized members who are not ordained|Bishops|Priests|Deacons|0|CCC 897.
Deacons serve in…|Charity and the word|Teaching only|Voting|Business|0|CCC 1570.
lessons.life: Say a prayer for your pastor.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: a pope who loved young people and traveled all over the world.
misc: “Only priests and nuns have jobs in the Church.”
lessons.mem: “We are many parts, but one body in Christ.” (see Romans 12:5)
lessons.hook: Show a body outline and ask: “What if the foot said it wasn’t needed?” Read 1 Corinthians 12:12–14. Ask what each part of the Church does.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name three roles in the Church and what each does.

script.open: Draw a big family tree on the board with names of a family. Ask, “How is this family organized? Who is the grandparent? Who is the parent?” Say, “The Church is a family, too, with different roles.”
teach: Say: “Jesus chose twelve apostles, with Peter as their leader. He said to Peter, ‘You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church.’ Peter was the first pope. Pope means ‘father.’ The Pope today is Peter’s successor, the Bishop of Rome. He leads the whole Church, teaches the faith and keeps us united.”

Say: “The bishops are the successors of the apostles. Each one leads a diocese, a local area. Your bishop is the leader of the Church in your area. Priests and deacons help the bishops, teach and celebrate the sacraments. Priests lead parishes. And all the rest of the baptized people are the laity, from the Greek word for ‘people.’ You are part of the laity!”

Read 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 in short form. Say: “Paul says that the Church is like a body, with many parts. The eye can’t say to the hand, ‘I don’t need you.’ Each part is important. All of us share Jesus’ mission: to love God and others, and to tell the world about Jesus. Laypeople are teachers, doctors, parents, farmers, and each can bring Jesus to their place.”
ask: Who is the Pope? What is his job? (The leader of the whole Church, Peter’s successor.)
Who leads the diocese? (The bishop.) The parish? (The priest.)
What is the job of the laity? (To bring Jesus to the world: at home, school and work.)
practice: Draw a chart on a large sheet: Jesus at the top; below him Peter and the apostles; then the Pope; the bishops; priests and deacons; and the laity.
Find out the name of the current Pope and your local bishop, and add them.
Write one job beside each level.
Add your own name under “the laity” and a way you can serve.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless our Pope, our bishop and our priests.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the Pope and our bishop by name.”

tryit: Build the Church family tree.
Find your bishop’s name.
Say what each member does.
lessons.saintStory:
Karol Wojtyła was born in Poland in 1920. He loved sports, theater and the mountains. As a young man, during World War II, he worked in a quarry and a factory, and he secretly studied for the priesthood when it was forbidden. He became a priest, then a bishop and cardinal.
In 1978 he was elected pope and took the name John Paul II. He was the first non-Italian pope in over four hundred years. He traveled to over a hundred countries, kissing the ground when he arrived. He started World Youth Day, inviting young people from all over the world, and he said to them, “Be not afraid!” In 1981 he was shot, and later he visited the man who shot him in prison and forgave him.
He died in 2005, and was named a saint in 2014. As Pope he shows how the leader of the Church serves the whole family.

lessons.title: Mary, Mother of God
lessons.idea: Mary is the Mother of God because her Son Jesus is God. She believed God’s word, said yes at the Annunciation, and stood by Jesus to the cross. She is also our mother, and we honor her and ask her to pray for us.
lessons.question: What does Mary teach us about faith?
lessons.activity: “Mary’s yes” frieze (25 min). Divide Mary’s life into six panels: Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Finding in the Temple, Cana, the Cross. Each group paints a panel and writes one thing Mary teaches. Pray the Hail Mary together slowly, noting its two halves (the angel’s words and our petition).
teach: Mary is “Theotokos,” Mother of God, because Jesus is God (CCC 495). The Church honors her above all other saints but never worships her (CCC 971).
Mary is a model of faith. At Cana she says, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). At the Cross she shares Jesus’ suffering. At Pentecost she prays with the apostles.
At the Cross Jesus gave her to John, and to all of us, as mother (John 19:26–27; CCC 501, 963). We ask her to pray for us as we ask any friend.
Some children’s families are not Catholic. Explain that honoring Mary honors Jesus.
talk: How do we pray the Hail Mary?
quiz: Mary is the Mother of…|God|Peter|Joseph|The apostles|0|CCC 495.
At Cana Mary said, “Do…”|Run|Nothing|Stay|Whatever he tells you|3|John 2:5.
The Hail Mary comes from…|A movie|Scripture and the Church|A game|A school|1|Luke 1.
lessons.life: Pray a decade of the Rosary.
lessons.saint: Bernard of Clairvaux: a monk who loved Mary and called her the Star of the Sea.
lessons.mem: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
lessons.hook: Ask children who taught them to say “yes” when it was hard. Show a picture of the Annunciation and ask what Mary says. Read Luke 1:38.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Why is Mary called Mother of God? What does she teach us?”

script.open: Show a photo of a mother and child. Ask, “What is special about a mom? Mary was the mom of Jesus. Think about how many moments she was there for him, from the beginning to the end.”
teach: Say: “Mary is the Mother of God. This does not mean that she is older than God, or that she is the source of God’s divinity. It means that her Son, Jesus, is God. A mother is the mother of the whole person, not just the body. Mary’s Son is a divine Person. So Mary is truly the Mother of God. The Church taught this at the Council of Ephesus in 431.”

Read Luke 1:39-56 in summary: “When Mary heard she would be the mother of the Savior, she went quickly to visit her cousin Elizabeth. Elizabeth said, ‘Blessed are you among women. Why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ And Mary sang the Magnificat: ‘My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord.’ She said yes at the Annunciation, she gave birth to Jesus, she presented him in the Temple, she found him at twelve, she was at Cana, and she stood by the cross.”

Say: “Jesus gave Mary to us from the cross: ‘Behold your mother.’ She is our spiritual mother. She prays for us and leads us to Jesus. We honor Mary. We do not worship her. We worship only God. We ask her to pray for us, because she is close to God.”
ask: Why is Mary called the Mother of God? (Because Jesus is God.)
What did Mary say at the Annunciation? (Yes, let it be done.)
What do we do when we honor Mary? (Ask her to pray for us, imitate her faith.)
practice: Fold a long paper into six panels for a frieze.
Label them: Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Finding in the Temple, Cana, the Cross.
Draw a scene in each and write a sentence about what Mary does.
Hang the frieze, and walk along it saying the Hail Mary at each panel.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray a Hail Mary tonight and ask Mary to pray for your family.”
