tryit: Make the six panels of Mary’s life.
Say what Mary does in each.
Pray the Hail Mary.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernard was born in 1090 in France to a noble family. When he was twenty-two, he went to a poor monastery at Cîteaux with thirty of his friends and relatives, and asked to become a monk. A few years later he started a new monastery at Clairvaux, in a wild valley, and became its abbot.
Bernard was a gifted preacher and writer, and kings and popes asked him for advice. He loved Mary deeply. In a well-known sermon he said that when we are tossed about like a boat on the sea of life, we should “look to the star, call on Mary.” People call Mary the “Star of the Sea” from this.
Bernard is called a Doctor of the Church. He shows us how to love Mary: not as a goddess, but as the mother who leads us to Jesus.

lessons.title: The communion of saints
lessons.idea: The communion of saints is the whole family of God: the faithful on earth, those being purified in purgatory, and the saints in heaven. We pray for each other, and the saints pray for us.
lessons.question: Who prays for you?
lessons.activity: “Three circles” (25 min). Draw three concentric circles: earth, purgatory, heaven. Children write names in each: people they pray for, people who have died they pray for, saints they ask to pray for them. Read Hebrews 12:1 (“a great cloud of witnesses”). Pray the Litany of the Saints in a short form.
teach: The Church is one family in Christ, in three states: pilgrims on earth, souls being purified, and saints in glory (CCC 954).
Saints are people who lived heroic love and now see God (CCC 828, 956). They pray for us, and we can ask for their help (CCC 956–957).
We pray for the dead, especially at Mass and on All Souls (November 2). Purgatory is the final cleansing of those who die in God’s friendship (CCC 1030–1031).
Be gentle with children who have lost someone. Say that love does not end.
quiz: The communion of saints includes…|All God’s holy people|Only monks|Only living|Only canonized|0|CCC 946.
Purgatory is…|A hotel|A place of despair|A cleansing|A prison|2|CCC 1030.
Saints pray…|Never|Against us|For us|Only for angels|2|CCC 956.
lessons.life: Write a litany with names of saints and family members.
lessons.saint: Perpetua: a young mother who held on to Jesus, and her friend Felicity.
misc: “Praying to saints takes away from Jesus.”
“Only people in heaven are in the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses…” (Hebrews 12:1)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of family members, some far away or who have died. Ask, “Are they still part of your family?” Introduce the idea that God’s family stretches beyond what we see.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the three parts of the communion of saints and one person to pray for.

script.open: Say, “Who prays for you? Make a list in your mind. Now, here is a surprise: even people you have never met pray for you. Let’s learn how.”
teach: Say: “We believe in the communion of saints. We say it in the Apostles’ Creed. It means that all of God’s people are one family, united in Jesus, whether they are alive on earth or have died. There are three parts of this family. The Church on earth: all of us still on our journey. The Church in purgatory: souls who died in God’s friendship, but are being cleansed before heaven. And the Church in heaven: the saints, who see God face to face.”

Say: “Death doesn’t end the family. Hebrews 12:1 says, ‘We are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses.’ We pray for each other. The saints in heaven pray for us. And we can pray for the souls in purgatory, to help them reach heaven. We do this especially on All Souls’ Day, November 2, and at every Mass.”

Say: “Why do we ask saints to pray for us? For the same reason we ask a friend: ‘Please pray for me.’ The saints are alive in Christ, closer to God than we are, and their prayers are powerful. They are not ‘in between’ us and God. They pray with us. And on All Saints’ Day, November 1, we celebrate all of them.”
ask: What does ‘communion of saints’ mean? (The whole family of God: on earth, in purgatory, in heaven.)
How do we help those in purgatory? (By praying for them, and having Masses offered.)
Why do we ask saints to pray for us? (They are alive in Christ and close to God.)
practice: Draw three concentric circles on paper and label them earth, purgatory and heaven.
Write names in each: people you are praying for, people who have died that you want to pray for, and saints you love.
Say a short prayer for each name, “Lord, grant them peace,” or “Saint ____, pray for us.”
Keep the sheet as a prayer list.
script.close: Pray the Eternal Rest prayer: “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say the Eternal Rest prayer for someone who has died.”

tryit: Draw three circles: earth, purgatory, heaven.
Write names in each.
Pray for someone in each circle.
lessons.saintStory:
Perpetua was a young, well-educated woman in Carthage, North Africa, around the year 203. She had a baby son, and she was a catechumen, learning to become a Christian. The Roman government had made it illegal to become one. She and a few friends were arrested, including Felicity, a slave who was expecting a baby.
Perpetua’s father begged her to give up her faith for the sake of her child. She said, “Father, do you see this vase? Can it be called by any other name than what it is?” He said no. “Neither can I call myself anything other than what I am: a Christian.” She wrote a diary in prison, one of the earliest writings by a Christian woman. She and Felicity were put to death for their faith, and the Christians of Carthage told their story.
Perpetua and Felicity are named in the Mass. They are part of the communion of saints, praying for us.

lessons.title: Heaven and eternal life
lessons.idea: God made us to be with him forever. Heaven is perfect life with God, and Jesus opened it to us. Our choices matter: we can choose God or turn away. God offers mercy, and we hope to be with him forever.
lessons.question: What does it mean to choose God?
lessons.activity: “Road to heaven” map (25 min). Children draw a winding road with signs for choices (honest word, helping a friend, sharing, praying) that lead toward a bright city and signs (lying, hurting) that lead away, and a path back (sorry, Confession). Read Revelation 21:1–4. Talk about how Jesus helps us stay on the road.
teach: Heaven is the fulfillment of our deepest longing: to see God and live with him (CCC 1023–1026). It is a life of love and joy that has no end.
God desires all to be saved (CCC 1058). We can freely refuse him. Hell is the choice to stay away from God forever (CCC 1033–1037). Speak gently and briefly with children.
After death each person is judged by Christ (CCC 1021–1022). We trust in his mercy and live for him now.
Do not use fear. Teach that the aim of the Christian life is love of God and joy.
talk: What does it mean to choose God?
What do you hope for in heaven?
How can you help others get there?
quiz: Heaven is…|Rest only|Life with God|A cloud|A place of toys|1|CCC 1024.
Our choices…|Are forced|Don’t matter|Matter|Are random|2|CCC 1033.
God wants all to be…|Famous|Rich|Saved|Lost|2|1 Timothy 2:4.
lessons.life: Make a thank-you card to someone who helped you.
lessons.saint: Stephen: the first martyr, who saw heaven open.
lessons.mem: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” (Revelation 21:4)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What is the best party you can imagine?” Then read Revelation 21:4 aloud. Explain that heaven is even better because God is there.
lessons.assess: Ask children to say what heaven is and one choice that leads toward God.

script.open: Hold up a drawing of a road, with a signpost, going up a hill. Ask, “Where do you think this road leads? What would you hope to find at the end?” Let them guess. “Today we talk about the end of our road.”
teach: Say: “God made us to be with him forever. That is what heaven is: perfect life with God, in joy, forever. Revelation 21:3-4 says: ‘God himself will be with them. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore.’ In heaven, there is no suffering. We will see God face to face. We will be with Mary, the angels, the saints and our loved ones. And we will be perfectly happy.”

Say: “Jesus opened heaven for us by his death and Resurrection. Before him, heaven was closed. Now it is open to all who love him. But we are free. God does not force us. We can choose God or turn away. Our choices matter. Every time we choose to love, we move closer to him.”

Say: “God is merciful. If we are sorry, he forgives us. We hope to be with him. And we do not know the day we will die, so we try to live every day in his friendship. We pray, we go to Mass and Confession, and we care for others. Heaven isn’t a faraway dream. It begins now, in our relationship with God.”
ask: What is heaven? (Perfect life with God forever.)
Who opened heaven for us? (Jesus.)
How can we get ready for heaven? (Choose good, pray, receive the sacraments, love others.)
practice: Give each child a large sheet of paper. Say: “Draw a winding road that leads to a bright place at the top, heaven.”
Along the road, draw signs for good choices: an honest word, helping a friend, sharing, praying.
Draw one side road that leads away. Label it with a bad choice, and add a sign: “Turn back: God forgives.”
Show a partner the map and explain it.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, lead us to heaven.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family how you can help each other get to heaven.”

tryit: Draw a road to heaven.
Put signs on it: honest word, help a friend, share, pray.
Add one turn that leads away.
lessons.saintStory:
Stephen was one of seven men chosen by the apostles to help care for the poor in the early Church in Jerusalem. The Bible says he was “full of faith and the Holy Spirit.” He did great wonders and spoke so wisely that people could not argue with him.
Some people in the city became angry with him. They took him to the council and brought false witnesses to lie about him. When Stephen spoke, he told the whole story of God’s people, and said that they had not listened to God’s prophets. This made them furious.
The Bible says that Stephen, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said, “I see the heavens opened!” As he was being stoned, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” and “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Stephen shows what heaven means for us: even in death, God is waiting.

units.title: The sacraments
units.eq: How do the sacraments help us?

lessons.title: What is a sacrament?
lessons.idea: A sacrament is an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives us God’s grace. The Church has seven: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony.
lessons.question: Name the seven sacraments.
lessons.activity: “Seven signs” gallery (30 min). Seven stations with a real object each (water, chrism oil or scented oil, bread, a stole, oil of the sick, a ring, a candle). Children match each to its sacrament and write the sign and the grace. Make an accordion book of the seven.
teach: A sacrament is “an efficacious sign of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church” (CCC 1131). It uses material things (water, oil, bread) and words.
The seven are grouped: sacraments of initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), of healing (Reconciliation, Anointing), of service (Holy Orders, Matrimony) (CCC 1210–1211).
The sacraments are ways Christ touches us today, as he touched the sick in the Gospels (Mark 6:56; CCC 1115–1116).
Do not reduce sacraments to ceremonies. They are encounters with Jesus.
quiz: A sacrament is…|A story|An outward sign that gives grace|A party|A ritual only|1|CCC 1131.
Baptism uses…|Bread|Incense|Water|Oil|2|CCC 1214.
The seven sacraments were instituted by…|Saints|Christ|Bishops|The Pope|1|CCC 1114.
lessons.life: List the seven sacraments from memory.
lessons.saint: Ambrose: the bishop who taught new Christians about the sacraments and baptized Augustine.
misc: “You earn grace by doing sacraments right.”
lessons.mem: The seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, Matrimony.
lessons.hook: Show a handshake, a hug and a ring. Ask what each means. Explain that signs do something real. Sacraments are signs that actually give what they show.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name all seven and match two with their signs.

script.open: Show a wedding ring. Ask, “What does this mean? It is a sign of a promise. But it is more than a sign: it actually binds two people together.” Say, “Today we learn about special signs that give us something real.”
teach: Say: “A sacrament is an outward sign, given by Jesus, that gives us grace. An outward sign is something we can see, touch, hear or smell, like water, oil, bread or words. Grace is God’s free gift of his own life. Jesus gave the Church seven sacraments. We use ordinary things, and God does something wonderful.”

Say: “Jesus often used physical things in his miracles. He touched people. He made mud. He took bread. In John 3:5 he said, ‘Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’ Today, Jesus acts through the sacraments. In Mark 6:56, people were healed just by touching the hem of his cloak. We meet Jesus in the sacraments.”

Say: “The seven sacraments are: Baptism (water), Confirmation (oil called chrism), Eucharist (bread and wine), Reconciliation (words of forgiveness), Anointing of the Sick (oil), Holy Orders (laying on of hands), and Matrimony (exchange of vows). Each one gives grace for a special need. God does the work: the sacrament works because of Christ.”
ask: What is a sacrament? (An outward sign, given by Christ, that gives grace.)
What is grace? (God’s free gift of his life and help.)
Name the seven sacraments. (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing, Orders, Matrimony.)
practice: Set up seven stations, each with a real object: a bowl of water, a bottle of scented oil, bread and a cup, a stole, a small jar of oil, a candle or ring, a wedding ring.
Give children a gallery card for each. They visit, look and touch, and write the sacrament’s name, and what it gives.
Rotate every four minutes.
Gather to share one thing each station taught.
script.close: Pray: “Lord Jesus, thank you for the sacraments.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Name the seven sacraments to your family.”

tryit: Visit the seven stations.
Touch and look at each sign.
Say what each gives.
lessons.saintStory:
Ambrose was born around the year 339, the son of a high Roman official. He studied law and became governor of northern Italy, based in Milan. When the bishop of Milan died, the people were arguing about who should be the next bishop. Ambrose came to calm them down, and a child (or someone in the crowd) shouted, “Ambrose for bishop!” and everyone agreed.
He wasn’t even baptized yet! Within a week he was baptized, ordained and made bishop. He gave his wealth to the poor and spent his time studying the Bible. He preached well, and a young teacher named Augustine came to hear him, and Ambrose baptized him on Easter in 387.
Ambrose wrote to the newly baptized about the sacraments, explaining how God works through signs, like water, oil, bread and wine. He shows how God uses physical things to give his grace.

lessons.title: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist
lessons.idea: Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist are the sacraments of initiation. They bring us into the Church, make us God’s children, strengthen us with the Spirit and feed us with Jesus’ Body and Blood.
lessons.question: What do the three have in common?
lessons.activity: “Door, strength, meal” (25 min). Draw a church door (Baptism: new life in water), a flame (Confirmation: Spirit’s seal), a table (Eucharist: food for the journey). Under each, write the sign (water, oil, bread and wine), the words and the gift. Read Acts 2:38–42.
teach: Baptism frees us from original sin, makes us children of God and members of the Church (CCC 1213, 1250). The sign is water and the words “I baptize you in the name of the Father…”
Confirmation seals us with the gift of the Holy Spirit through anointing with chrism (CCC 1285, 1302–1303). The Eucharist is the source and summit of Christian life (CCC 1324).
These three are received in a different order depending on your Church: in the Latin Church, Baptism, then First Communion and Confirmation (or Confirmation first in some places). Check your diocese.
Invite families to share their baptism stories and photos.
talk: What do they have in common?
quiz: Confirmation uses…|Chrism oil|Salt|Bread|Water|0|CCC 1293.
The Eucharist is…|Source and summit|A symbol|A treat|Optional|0|CCC 1324.
Baptism is the…|Door|Floor|Window|Roof|0|CCC 1213.
lessons.life: Look at photos of your baptism and thank God.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a missionary who baptized many people in India and Japan.
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Show a school ID, a team jersey and a key. Ask: “How do you join something?” Explain that these three sacraments “join” us to Jesus and his family.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the three and the sign of each.

script.open: Draw a door on the board. Ask, “What happens when you walk through a door? You go into a new place. Today we will see three sacraments that welcome us into God’s family.”
teach: Say: “The sacraments of initiation are Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist. ‘Initiation’ means beginning, entering. These three sacraments bring us into the Church. They are the way we become full members of God’s family. Adults receive all three at the Easter Vigil. Children often receive them over several years.”

Read Acts 2:38-42 briefly. Say: “On Pentecost, Peter said to the crowd, ‘Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.’ About three thousand were baptized and joined the apostles, to share the breaking of bread and prayers.”

Say: “Baptism is the door. We are washed with water, our sins are forgiven, and we become children of God. Confirmation is the strength. The bishop (or priest) anoints us with oil called chrism and says, ‘Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.’ We are strengthened to live our faith. The Eucharist is the meal. We receive Jesus’ Body and Blood, to feed our souls. Baptism is once for all, and so is Confirmation. We receive the Eucharist again and again.”
ask: What are the three sacraments of initiation? (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist.)
What does Baptism give us? (New life, forgiveness, becoming God’s children.)
How is the Eucharist different from the other two? (We receive it over and over.)
practice: Give each child a paper with three boxes labeled Door, Flame and Table.
Draw a church door for Baptism, a flame for Confirmation, a table with bread and a cup for the Eucharist.
Under each picture write a sentence about what it gives.
Share with a partner, then say together: “Door, strength, meal.”
script.close: Pray: “Thank you, God, for bringing us into your family.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your parents about your baptism, and your First Communion plans.”

tryit: Draw a door, a flame and a table.
Write what each sacrament gives.
Tell a partner.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis Xavier was born in 1506 in Spain, in a castle. He went to the University of Paris, where he met a student named Ignatius of Loyola, and became one of the first Jesuits.
He sailed to India in 1541, a voyage that took over a year. He walked from village to village, ringing a little bell to gather the children. He taught them the Our Father, the Creed and the Commandments, and baptized many people. He worked among the poor, the sick and the pearl divers. Then he traveled to Japan, and set out for China, but he died on an island off the coast in 1552.
He is the patron of missionaries. Francis Xavier shows how Baptism brings people into God’s family, and how the sacraments are for everyone.

lessons.title: Reconciliation, Anointing, Orders, Matrimony
lessons.idea: Reconciliation and the Anointing of the Sick heal us in body and soul, and Holy Orders and Matrimony are for service: priests serve God’s people, and husband and wife serve each other and their children.
lessons.question: How does each sacrament help the Church?
lessons.activity: “Healing and service” sort (25 min). Cards with scenes (a sick grandfather, a child who lied, a wedding, an ordination). Children sort into Healing or Service and name the sacrament, minister and sign. Role-play a simple Confession examination (“Did I hurt someone? Did I tell the truth?”).
teach: In Reconciliation, the priest acts in Christ’s name to forgive sins (CCC 1421–1424). The sign is the penitent’s confession, the priest’s absolution and the penance.
In the Anointing of the Sick, the priest anoints the forehead and hands with oil and prays for strength and healing (CCC 1499–1513, James 5:14–15).
Holy Orders gives bishops, priests and deacons their ministry (CCC 1536). Matrimony makes a man and a woman a lifelong covenant of love open to children (CCC 1601–1603).
Introduce Confession as a gift. Reassure children that the priest is bound to secrecy.
talk: How do these help the Church?
quiz: Anointing of the Sick helps…|Priests|The seriously ill|Teachers|Healthy people|1|CCC 1499.
Holy Orders makes…|Teachers|Bishops, priests, deacons|Kings|Doctors|1|CCC 1536.
Matrimony is…|A lifelong covenant|A short promise|A party|A game|0|CCC 1601.
lessons.life: Pray for priests and married couples.
lessons.saint: Camillus de Lellis: a soldier turned nurse who started hospitals for the sick.
misc: “The Anointing of the Sick is only for people who are dying.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, I am sorry for my sins. Help me to do better.” (a child’s Act of Contrition, simple form)
lessons.hook: Show a first-aid kit and a toolbox. “One mends, one builds.” The sacraments of healing mend us; the sacraments of service build up the Church.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to match a need with the sacrament that helps.

script.open: Place a bandage, a ring and a stole on a table. Ask, “What do these three things have in common? They all show how God cares for us at special times in our lives.”
teach: Say: “There are two sacraments of healing. Reconciliation, also called Confession or Penance, heals our soul when we have sinned. We tell our sins to a priest, we say we are sorry, and the priest forgives us in the name of Jesus. Anointing of the Sick heals us when we are seriously ill, or old. The priest anoints the forehead and hands with oil and prays. It gives strength, peace and courage, forgives sins, and sometimes brings healing.”

Read James 5:14-15: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up.” Say: “Anointing of the Sick is for anyone who is in danger because of sickness or old age. It is not only for people who are dying.”

Say: “There are also two sacraments of service. Holy Orders: Jesus calls some men to be bishops, priests and deacons, to serve God’s people, teach, and celebrate the sacraments. Matrimony: a man and a woman promise to love each other for life, and God gives them the grace to be faithful. They serve each other and their children. All the sacraments are for others, but these two are especially for helping others get to heaven.”
ask: What are the two sacraments of healing? (Reconciliation and Anointing of the Sick.)
What are the two sacraments of service? (Holy Orders and Matrimony.)
What does the priest use in the Anointing of the Sick? (Blessed oil.)
practice: Prepare scene cards: a grandfather in the hospital; a child who told a lie; a wedding; a young man being ordained.
Make two headings: “Healing” and “Service.”
Children sort the cards, then name the sacrament for each and say what it gives.
Choose one scene and draw or act it out.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, heal us and help us serve.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone who is sick.”

tryit: Sort the scene cards: healing or service.
Match each to a sacrament.
Say what each gives.
lessons.saintStory:
Camillus was born in Italy in 1550. He grew up tall and strong, and became a soldier, and a gambler who lost everything. A sore on his leg that would not heal sent him to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, where he worked as a servant. But he was fired for gambling.
Soon after, when he was twenty-five, he decided to change his life. He returned to the hospital, and began to care for the patients, as a nurse. He saw how poorly the sick were treated, so he started a group of men who would care for the sick as a mother cares for her child. Their uniform was a black habit with a red cross on the chest. It is the origin of the Red Cross symbol.
Camillus also became a priest. He is the patron saint of nurses and the sick. He shows how Anointing of the Sick, and love for the sick, bring Jesus’ healing.

lessons.title: Why we pray
lessons.idea: Prayer is raising our hearts and minds to God. God invites us to pray, and he always hears us. We can pray anywhere, anytime, with words or in silence.
lessons.question: When is it easy to pray?
lessons.activity: “Prayer rhythms” (20 min). Children draw a day: morning, meals, school, bedtime. For each, they write a short prayer (Morning Offering, Grace, Guardian Angel, Examen). They practice a minute of silence and share how it felt. Read Luke 11:1–4.
teach: Prayer is “the raising of one’s mind and heart to God” (CCC 2559). It is a gift: God thirsts that we may thirst for him (CCC 2560).
Jesus taught the Our Father when his friends asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). We learn to pray by praying.
Prayer has many forms but one meaning: a relationship. Good habits (a regular time, a quiet place) help (CCC 2691).
Many children think prayer is only asking for things. Introduce listening and thanking.
quiz: Prayer is…|Raising the mind and heart to God|A trick|A chore|A speech|0|CCC 2559.
God hears…|Only the loud|Only the long|Only the good|Every prayer|3|Psalm 34.
To pray we need…|Fancy words|An open heart|A special place|A priest|1|CCC 2562.
lessons.life: Set a prayer time and keep it for a week.
lessons.saint: Ephrem the Syrian: a deacon who wrote hymns and prayers that are still used.
misc: “God only answers if I pray the right words.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Show a phone. Ask who calls them when they are away. “Prayer is a call to someone who loves us and always answers.” Pause for a moment of silence together.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name when they will pray and what they will say.

script.open: Say, “Pretend you are on the phone with your best friend. What do you do? You talk, you listen, you share news. Prayer is a conversation like that with God.” Let the children share about phone or video calls.
teach: Say: “Prayer means raising our hearts and minds to God. We talk to him, and we listen. God invites us to pray, and he always hears us. Jesus’ own friends asked, ‘Lord, teach us to pray,’ and he taught them the Our Father. (Luke 11:1-4) Prayer is not just words. It is spending time with someone who loves us.”

Say: “We can pray anywhere, anytime: in a church, in a car, in bed, at the beach. We can pray with words, with songs or in silence. We can use prayers we know by heart, or our own words. God is always listening. Why should we pray? Because we are made for God, and prayer is how we grow closer. Without it, any friendship dies.”

Say: “Prayer is not just asking for things. It is also thanking, praising, saying sorry and listening. And prayer works. Not always as we expect, but God answers with what is best for us. A good habit is to pray at set times, like morning and bedtime, and before meals. The Church also gives us prayers like the Morning Offering, the Our Father and the Hail Mary.”
ask: What is prayer? (Raising our hearts and minds to God.)
When can we pray? (Always, anywhere.)
What are some good times to pray? (Morning, meals, bedtime, when worried.)
practice: Give each child a paper divided into four sections: morning, meals, school, bedtime.
In each section, draw a picture, and write a short prayer: “Morning Offering,” “Bless us, O Lord,” “Come, Holy Spirit,” “Angel of God.”
Take turns reading a prayer to a partner.
Choose one to start doing this week.
script.close: Pray the Sign of the Cross, and the Morning Offering: “O Jesus, through the Immaculate Heart of Mary, I offer you my prayers, works, joys and sufferings of this day.” Send home: “Use your prayer chart this week.”

tryit: Draw your day.
Write a short prayer for each part.
Choose one to pray each day.
lessons.saintStory:
Ephrem was born around the year 306 in the city of Nisibis, in what is now Turkey. He became a deacon, a helper to the bishop, and a teacher. He wrote many poems, hymns and homilies in his own language, Syriac, to teach the faith and to praise God.
When a war forced him to leave his home, he settled in the city of Edessa and kept writing. He taught that creation is full of signs of God, like a book. He helped the poor, and during a famine he organized relief. People loved to sing his hymns, even when some false teachers copied the melodies, so he wrote new, true words.
Ephrem is called the Harp of the Holy Spirit. He wrote a prayer that Christians still pray in Lent: “O Lord and Master of my life, take from me the spirit of sloth.” He shows us that prayer can be made of words and songs.

lessons.title: Kinds of prayer
lessons.idea: The Church names five kinds of prayer: blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving and praise. We can pray aloud (vocal prayer), by thinking about God’s word (meditation), or by resting in his love (contemplation).
lessons.question: What kind of prayer do you pray most?
lessons.activity: “Five forms” prayer corners (25 min). Five corners, each with a card and a way to pray: bless/adore (kneel and be quiet), petition (write one need), intercession (write a name), thanks (list three thanks), praise (sing or read Psalm 150). Rotate; then compose a class prayer using all five.
teach: Five forms of prayer (CCC 2626–2643): adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise. Each has a place in the Mass.
Three expressions of prayer (CCC 2700–2724): vocal, meditation, contemplation. Meditation uses thought and imagination; contemplation is simple presence.
Psalm 150 is a prayer of praise. The psalms are the prayer book of Jesus and the Church (CCC 2585–2589).
Remind children that sorry (contrition) belongs to prayer too. It appears at the Mass and in Confession.
quiz: Adoration says…|God is great|Please|Sorry|Thank you|0|CCC 2628.
Intercession is…|Singing|Praying for ourselves|Not praying|Praying for others|3|CCC 2634.
Thanksgiving says…|Please|Thank you|Hello|Sorry|1|CCC 2637.
lessons.life: Pray for someone by name every day.
lessons.saint: Hildegard of Bingen: an abbess who praised God in music.
misc: “If God doesn’t give me what I ask, prayer doesn’t work.”
lessons.mem: “Praise the Lord! Praise God in his sanctuary.” (Psalm 150:1)
lessons.hook: Play five short clips (or act): saying “wow” at a sunset, asking a parent for help, asking help for a friend, saying thank you, shouting for joy at a game. “Which is prayer?” Each can be.
lessons.assess: Ask children to match five prayer lines with their kinds.

script.open: Play a minute of beautiful music, such as a chant or a song of praise. Say, “How does it make you feel? Music can lift our hearts to God. It is one way to pray.”
teach: Read Psalm 150 aloud. Say: “‘Praise the Lord! Praise God in his sanctuary… Praise him with trumpet sound, praise him with lute and harp… Let everything that breathes praise the Lord!’ The Psalms are the prayer book of God’s people. Jesus prayed them. They teach us different ways to pray.”

Say: “The Catechism names five forms of prayer. Blessing and adoration: we bless God, who blesses us, and we adore him as our Creator. Petition: we ask God for what we need, and sorry for our sins. Intercession: we pray for others. Thanksgiving: we thank God for everything. Praise: we praise God just because he is God. Many prayers include more than one.”

Say: “There are also three ways to express prayer. Vocal prayer uses words, aloud or in our minds, like the Our Father. Meditation is thinking about God’s word, such as imagining a Gospel scene and asking, ‘What is Jesus saying to me?’ Contemplation is resting in God’s love, quietly, without many words, like sitting with someone you love. All three are good, and we can use them all.”
ask: Name the five forms of prayer. (Blessing/adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise.)
What is vocal prayer? (Prayer in words.)
How is meditation different from contemplation? (Meditation thinks about God’s word; contemplation rests in his love.)
practice: Set up five corners, each with a card: Bless/Adore (kneel and be quiet), Petition (write a request), Intercession (write a name of someone to pray for), Thanksgiving (write three thank-yous), Praise (sing or say, “Alleluia!”).
Groups spend about four minutes at each corner.
At each, they pray in that way.
Gather and say one prayer from each corner aloud.
script.close: Pray the Our Father together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Try a different kind of prayer each day.”

tryit: Visit each of the five prayer corners.
Pray in the way shown.
Write a prayer for each.
lessons.saintStory:
Hildegard was born in 1098 in Germany, the tenth child of a noble family. When she was eight years old, her parents offered her to the Church, and she went to live with a holy woman next to a monastery. She grew up to be an abbess, and led a community of nuns.
Hildegard had visions of God, which she wrote down, and she also wrote about plants and medicine, and composed over seventy songs and a musical drama, in beautiful, soaring melodies. She wrote letters to popes, emperors and kings, and traveled to preach. She told people to praise God with music and to take care of the earth.
Hildegard is a Doctor of the Church. She shows how praise can be prayer, and how we can use gifts like music to worship.

lessons.title: The Rosary
lessons.idea: The Rosary is a prayer with Mary that helps us think about the life of Jesus. We pray Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes while meditating on 20 mysteries in four sets: joyful, luminous, sorrowful, glorious.
lessons.question: Which mystery speaks to you?
lessons.activity: “Make and pray” (30 min). Children make a decade rosary with ten beads, knot and cross. Teach how to hold it and say a decade, meditating on one mystery. Provide picture cards of the joyful mysteries. Pray one decade together slowly. Invite them to pray a decade at home with family.
teach: The Rosary is a Gospel prayer that follows Mary as she contemplates Christ (CCC 971, 2678, 2708). It has 20 mysteries in four sets (St John Paul II added the luminous mysteries in 2002).
The Hail Mary has two parts: the greeting of Gabriel and Elizabeth (Luke 1:28, 42) and the Church’s petition (CCC 2676–2677).
We do not repeat prayers mindlessly: like a song, the words support the heart. Encourage children to picture each scene.
Be kind to children who find sitting still hard; let them hold beads or follow with pictures.
talk: What do you think about while praying?
quiz: The Rosary meditates on…|A map|A recipe|The life of Jesus and Mary|A race|2|CCC 2708.
There are…|Four sets of mysteries|Ten sets|Two sets|One set|0|Rosarium Virginis Mariae.
The Rosary begins with…|The Gloria|The Hail Mary|The Sign of the Cross|The Amen|2|Tradition.
lessons.life: Pray one decade each day this week.
lessons.saint: Louis de Montfort: a priest who taught people to pray the Rosary.
misc: “You have to pray the whole Rosary every time.”
lessons.mem: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.
lessons.hook: Hold up a rosary and a string of beads from a craft kit. Ask what the beads are for. Show how they help us count prayers while our minds rest in Jesus.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the four sets of mysteries and one mystery from each.

script.open: Hold up a rosary and say, “What is this? What do people do with it?” Let children share. “It looks like jewelry, but it is a tool for prayer. It is like a spiritual road map.”
teach: Say: “The Rosary is a prayer with Mary. We say the Our Father, ten Hail Marys and the Glory Be, while thinking about moments in the life of Jesus and Mary, called mysteries. A set of ten Hail Marys is called a decade. A full Rosary has five decades. We use beads to keep count, so we can focus on the mysteries.”

Say: “There are twenty mysteries, in four sets. The Joyful Mysteries: the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the Presentation and the Finding in the Temple. The Luminous Mysteries (the mysteries of Light): the Baptism of Jesus, the Wedding at Cana, the Proclamation of the Kingdom, the Transfiguration and the Institution of the Eucharist. The Sorrowful Mysteries: the Agony in the Garden, the Scourging, the Crowning with Thorns, the Carrying of the Cross and the Crucifixion. The Glorious Mysteries: the Resurrection, the Ascension, the Descent of the Holy Spirit, the Assumption and the Coronation of Mary.”

Say: “Why do we pray it? When we say the words of the Hail Mary, our minds can rest on the story of Jesus. It is like looking at a photo album with Mary, who knows the story best. The Rosary is for everyone: it is simple enough for a child and deep enough for a saint. Many families pray it together.”
ask: What are the four sets of mysteries? (Joyful, Luminous, Sorrowful, Glorious.)
What is a decade? (Ten Hail Marys.)
Why do we use beads? (To count, so we can focus on the mystery.)
practice: Give each child ten beads, a short string or pipe cleaner, and a small cross.
Help them string the beads and tie knots, and attach the cross.
Show how to hold the rosary and pray one decade, starting with the Our Father, then ten Hail Marys, and the Glory Be.
Choose a mystery, such as the Nativity, and think about it silently while praying one decade together.
script.close: Pray a decade together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray a decade with someone at home.”

tryit: Make a one-decade rosary.
Learn how to pray a decade.
Think about a mystery.
lessons.saintStory:
Louis-Marie Grignion was born in France in 1673. He became a priest and spent his life traveling around western France, giving missions, which are weeks of preaching, in country parishes. He often walked, and slept in poor places.
Louis loved Mary, and he taught people to pray the Rosary. He gave out rosaries, led processions, and wrote a book called True Devotion to Mary. He taught that devotion to Mary leads us to Jesus. Some people didn’t like his message and he was sent away several times. He kept going. He died at forty-three, worn out from work.
Louis de Montfort shows how the Rosary can be a family prayer, for everyone, anywhere.

units.title: The Church year and Sunday
units.eq: How do we live the Church year?

lessons.title: Sunday and the Mass
lessons.idea: Sunday is the Lord’s Day, the day of Jesus’ Resurrection. Catholics gather at Mass on Sunday, hear God’s word, receive Jesus in the Eucharist, and rest and enjoy family. Missing Mass without a serious reason is a serious matter.
lessons.question: Why is Sunday special?
lessons.activity: “Make Sunday special” plan (25 min). Children design a Sunday poster with four boxes: Mass, rest, family, service. Brainstorm what each looks like (read a book, call a grandparent, visit someone). Write a family agreement they can bring home.
teach: The Lord’s Day is Sunday because Jesus rose on the first day of the week (CCC 2174). Christians gather for the Eucharist, “the source and summit” of Church life (CCC 2177–2178).
The Church obliges Catholics to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days unless excused for serious reasons such as illness (CCC 2180–2183).
Rest is also holy: we rest from unnecessary work so we can worship, spend time with family and enjoy God’s gifts (CCC 2184–2188).
Be sensitive: some families work on Sundays or lack transportation. Focus on desire, not blame.
talk: How does your family spend Sunday?
quiz: Sunday is…|A secret|The Lord’s Day|Saturday|A work day|1|CCC 2174.
We rest to…|Grow tired|Honor God|Hide|Sleep|1|CCC 2184.
Catholics must go to Mass on…|Sundays and holy days|Never|Fridays|Mondays|0|CCC 2180.
lessons.life: Keep one hour of Sunday free from screens.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Antioch: a bishop who wrote that Christians live by the Lord’s Day.
lessons.mem: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24)
lessons.hook: Ask what makes a day special (birthday, holiday). Ask what makes Sunday different. Show a calendar with Sundays circled in gold: “Every Sunday is a little Easter.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to say why Sunday is special and what they will do this Sunday.

script.open: Show a calendar with seven days. Ask, “Which day of the week is the most special? What do you do?” Let them share. “We’ll see how God made one day of the week extra special, and why.”
teach: Say: “Sunday is called the Lord’s Day. On Sunday morning, Jesus rose from the dead. That is why we gather on Sunday. The Psalm says, ‘This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.’ (Psalm 118:24) It is the first day of the week, and in a way it is the eighth day, a day for new creation.”

Say: “The third commandment says to keep holy the Sabbath. Christians do this on Sunday. On Sunday, Catholics are required to go to Mass, to hear God’s word, receive Jesus in Holy Communion, and give thanks together. Missing Mass without a serious reason, such as illness, is a serious matter, because we are neglecting our relationship with God and his family. We also rest from unnecessary work, and spend time with family.”

Say: “Sunday is a gift, not a burden. God knows that we need rest, joy and each other. The Mass is the high point of the week. And our week begins and ends around it. It’s also a good day for visiting grandparents, playing games together, going out in nature and helping others.”
ask: Why do Catholics go to Mass on Sunday? (It is the Lord’s Day, Jesus’ Resurrection.)
What do we do at Mass? (Hear God’s word, receive Jesus, give thanks.)
How can we make Sunday special? (Mass, rest, family, service.)
practice: Give each child a paper divided into four boxes: Mass, Rest, Family, Service.
Brainstorm what could go in each: wearing nice clothes, singing; a nap, a walk; a family meal, a game; visiting a neighbor, helping at the parish.
Each child writes or draws ideas in each box.
Take the poster home and ask the family to try it.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, thank you for Sunday.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make a plan for next Sunday.”

tryit: Design a Sunday poster.
Put Mass, rest, family and service in the four boxes.
Plan how to make Sunday special.
lessons.saintStory:
Ignatius was the bishop of Antioch, in Syria, a city where followers of Jesus were first called Christians. He lived about the year 100, and tradition says that he had known the apostle John.
When Ignatius was an old man, the Roman emperor ordered him arrested and taken to Rome to be killed in the arena. As he traveled, under guard, he wrote seven letters to churches along the way. He told the Christians to stay united with their bishop, to celebrate the Eucharist, and to love one another. He wrote that Christians no longer keep the Sabbath, but live by the Lord’s Day, when our life rose through Jesus.
He wrote to the Romans, begging them not to save him from martyrdom. Ignatius shows how early Christians loved Sunday, the Eucharist and the Church.

lessons.title: Seasons and colors
lessons.idea: The Church year retells the story of Jesus in seasons: Advent (purple), Christmas (white), Ordinary Time (green), Lent (purple), the Easter Triduum and Easter (white), and Pentecost (red). The colors of the priest’s vestments show the season.
lessons.question: What are the colors of the seasons?
lessons.activity: “Church year wheel” (30 min). Divide a paper plate or circle into seasons. Children color each section the right color, name the season, and write or draw one thing we do (wreath, manger, ashes, Easter candle). Display and use all year.
teach: The liturgical year unfolds the whole mystery of Christ from the Incarnation to the Lord’s return (CCC 1163–1167). Sunday is the heart of it, and Easter is the greatest feast (CCC 1168–1169).
Colors: purple (waiting and repentance), white (joy and purity), green (growth), red (Spirit and martyrs) (CCC 1155). Pink on two Sundays shows joy.
The year begins with Advent, not January 1. Three days before Easter, the Triduum, is the center.
Use your parish’s actual environment, e.g., take children to see the vestments or the paschal candle.
quiz: Advent is…|Red|White|Purple|Green|2|Liturgy.
Easter is…|Purple|Red|Black|White|3|Liturgy.
Pentecost is…|Green|Purple|Red|Black|2|Liturgy.
lessons.life: Mark the church year on your family calendar.
lessons.saint: Gregory the Great: a pope who shaped the Church’s prayer and music.
misc: “Lent is only about giving up candy.”
lessons.mem: “For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven.” (Ecclesiastes 3:1)
lessons.hook: Show a color wheel and colored fabric swatches. Say: “The Church tells the story of Jesus all year long, with colors.” Ask which color might mean joy, waiting, fire.
lessons.assess: Ask children to match seasons, colors and one tradition each.

script.open: Put four items on a table: a purple cloth, a white cloth, a green cloth, a red cloth. Say, “These are the colors the priest wears. Have you noticed that they change? They tell a story. Let’s learn it.”
teach: Say: “The Church’s year is not like the calendar year. It begins with Advent, in late November or early December. It tells the whole story of Jesus every year. Here are the seasons. Advent is four weeks of waiting for Jesus, and the color is purple. Christmas celebrates his birth, and the color is white. Ordinary Time is the time between, when we listen to Jesus’ teachings and grow, and the color is green. (‘Ordinary’ comes from ‘ordinal,’ meaning ‘numbered,’ the weeks are counted.)”

Say: “Lent is forty days before Easter. We pray, fast and give to the poor. The color is purple again. The Easter Triduum, the three days from Holy Thursday to Easter, is the holiest time. Then comes Easter, which is fifty days long, ending with Pentecost. The color is white, and on Pentecost it is red, for the fire of the Holy Spirit. Red is also used for martyrs. Isaiah 40:1-5 says: ‘Comfort, comfort my people… prepare the way of the Lord.’ That is Advent’s message.”

Say: “Why do we have seasons? Because we need time to remember and celebrate each part of Jesus’ life. They help us live the mysteries of our faith, not just hear about them. Just as nature has seasons, so does the Church. And the colors help us see it.”
ask: What color is Advent? (Purple.)
What is the longest season? (Ordinary Time.)
What does red mean? (The Holy Spirit, and martyrs.)
practice: Give each child a paper plate or a circle.
Divide it into sections: Advent, Christmas, Ordinary Time, Lent, Triduum and Easter, Pentecost.
Color each section the right color and write the name and one thing we do in that season.
Share the wheels, and hang them in the room.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help us walk with you all year.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Notice the color the priest wears next Sunday.”

tryit: Color the church year wheel.
Use the right colors.
Say what each season means.
lessons.saintStory:
Gregory was born in Rome around 540, to a rich family. He became the prefect, the chief official of the city. But after his father died, he turned his family home into a monastery and gave away his wealth.
In 590, when Rome was suffering from floods, plague and war, Gregory was chosen as pope. He didn’t want the job. He called himself “servant of the servants of God.” He fed the poor of the city, organized the Church’s lands, wrote books, and sent a group of monks to England to preach. He also is remembered for the chant, known as “Gregorian chant,” a simple, beautiful way to sing the Church’s prayers.
Gregory is called Gregory the Great. He shows how the liturgy, the Church’s worship, can be beautiful and orderly.

lessons.title: Holy days and the saints’ feasts
lessons.idea: Besides Sundays, the Church keeps feasts of Mary and the saints, and holy days of obligation when Catholics go to Mass. The saints’ feasts remind us that ordinary people can become holy with God’s help.
lessons.question: Which feasts does your parish celebrate?
lessons.activity: “My saint” cards (25 min). Each child picks a saint (by name day, patron of something, or heroes they like). They make a card with the saint’s picture, dates, how they loved God and a prayer. Then plan a “feast day” celebration for one of them.
teach: Holy days of obligation in the U.S.: Mary Mother of God (Jan 1), Ascension, Assumption (Aug 15), All Saints (Nov 1), Immaculate Conception (Dec 8), Christmas (CCC 1167, 2043). Check your diocese for changes.
On the feasts of saints the Church celebrates their “birthday into heaven” (CCC 1173). Their lives show different ways of following Christ.
Revelation 7:9 shows the “great multitude” of saints. The Church canonizes people whose holiness is certain, but there are countless unnamed saints.
Help each child see that holiness is for them too.
quiz: Dec 8 is…|All Saints|Immaculate Conception|Christmas|Easter|1|Liturgy.
Aug 15 is…|Assumption|Pentecost|Epiphany|Ascension|0|Liturgy.
Nov 1 is…|Easter|All Saints|All Souls|Christmas|1|Liturgy.
lessons.life: Celebrate a feast day with a special meal and prayer.
lessons.saint: Frances Xavier Cabrini: an immigrant who cared for other immigrants.
misc: “Saints are people who never did anything wrong.”
“Only holy days of obligation are important.”
lessons.mem: “Saints of God, come to their aid; hasten to meet them, angels of the Lord.” (from the funeral rite)
lessons.hook: Bring a calendar and open to your birthday. Ask which saint shares your day or name. Show how the Church has a feast almost every day.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to share a saint and one way that saint loved God.

script.open: Show a calendar with several feast days marked. Ask, “Which of these days do you know? Christmas, Easter… Did you know that almost every day of the year is the feast of a saint?” Show examples: Nicholas, Patrick, Francis.
teach: Say: “The Church celebrates special days besides Sunday. Some of them are feasts of Mary, like the Immaculate Conception on December 8, the Annunciation on March 25, and the Assumption on August 15. Others are feasts of saints, such as Saint Nicholas on December 6, and Saint Patrick on March 17. The Church remembers a saint on the day they died, which is their birthday into heaven.”

Say: “Some days are called holy days of obligation. These are special days besides Sunday when Catholics are required to go to Mass. In the United States they include Christmas (December 25), Mary, Mother of God (January 1), the Ascension, the Assumption (August 15), All Saints (November 1) and the Immaculate Conception (December 8). Check your own diocese, as some rules vary.”

Read Revelation 7:9-17 in summary. Say: “John saw a huge crowd from every nation, wearing white robes, praising God. They are the saints. The feasts of saints remind us that ordinary people, with God’s help, can become holy. A saint is not a perfect person. A saint is someone who kept trying, even after falling. And you can be a saint too.”
ask: What is a feast day? (A day to remember a saint, or an event in Jesus’ or Mary’s life.)
What is a holy day of obligation? (A special day when Catholics go to Mass.)
Who is your favorite saint, and why? (Take answers.)
practice: Give each child an index card, and a list of saints to choose from, or have children choose a saint by their name day, a patron of something they like, or a hero.
On the card, write: the saint’s name, the feast day, a virtue they showed, and a short prayer.
Add a small drawing.
Share cards in small groups. Collect them into a class “saints album.”
script.close: Pray: “Saints of God, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up your saint’s feast day and celebrate it.”

tryit: Pick a saint.
Make a saint card: name, feast day, a virtue and a prayer.
Share it.
lessons.saintStory:
Frances Cabrini was born in Italy in 1850, the youngest of thirteen children. She was small and often sick, but she wanted to be a missionary to China. She started a community of sisters, the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart.
The Pope sent her not to China, but to the United States, to help the many Italian immigrants arriving in New York. They were poor, often sick, and discriminated against. In 1889 she arrived with six sisters, and together they started schools, orphanages and hospitals in New York, Chicago, New Orleans, Seattle and many other cities. She crossed the ocean about thirty times.
She died in 1917, and was named the first American citizen to be a saint, in 1946. She is the patron of immigrants. She shows how an ordinary person with God’s help can do great things.
